This is the movie I always wanted to see in the theater. It's such a beautiful and amazing film, in so many ways … amazing cast, beautiful acting, mind-tripping cinematography, heartfelt storyline … and the love and family at the center of it all, tying everything together. Watching the film was a cathartic journey through the multiverse, I highly recommend going on this ride!

Everything Everywhere All at Once is exactly as overwhelming as it sounds: filled to the absolute brim with all the weird and wild in this universe and more. It's one of the most imaginative films in modern cinema and it was pure bliss to experience this in theaters. 

It's a testament to Daniels' writing that this film can throw googly eyes, hot dog fingers, and bagels at you while staying anchored by its emotional core. It is in these silly moments that the film disarms you, opens you up through laughter, and strikes you with earnest emotion while you're the most vulnerable. Before you know it, you're crying your eyes out to something as simple and stupid as two rocks falling on each other. Experiencing this film is ultimately a cathartic lesson that crying and laughing are not exclusive.

The story is just as moving as it is crazy. Everything Everywhere is a deep, thought-provoking, loving, and existential rumination on the decisions we make in life, all the paths we can but never take, all the sacrificed dreams, everything that leads us to everywhere, and still finding the love and empathy to make the world a better place. Even if our lives aren't what we hoped for, even if generational trauma has numbed us, even if we feel the unbearable weight of everything everywhere all at once, compassion is what pulls us through.
It’s a master piece! You have to watch it!

Part 1: Everything (The Cast) I can't believe it took this long for a massively talented actress like Michelle Yeoh to be the lead in an American film. The amount of talent that she garners from film to film is INSANE. She is BRILLIANT in this film, insanely amazing and epic. Her performance is so much fun. On the note of performances, MASSIVE kudos to the entirety of the cat, from Jamie Lee Curtis to the tin but AMAZING roles of Brian and Andy Le. Stephanie Hsu absolutely knocked the teeth out of the ballpark in this! Such a brutal performance for a character named Joy! Ke Huy Quan returns from his temporary retirement and I couldn't be more in love! He plays the many versions of Waymond Wang to perfection *chef kiss.* Jamie Lee Curtis is wild and unhinged. It's my favorite performance she's ever given, she needs a solo movie as this character, truly an absolutely spectacular casting! James Hong is 93 years old...... His performance is the best entertainment performance for a person above the age of 70 I've ever seen. In fact, I would put his performance here up in the middle-aged category, that's how much energy and life he brings to Gong Gong. Every single side character deserves to continue down a road towards a lead role in a major motion picture, they are absolutely groundbreakingly awesome. Every extra in this movie deserves to move on to playing side characters in Hollywood. Enough fan Girling about the amazing cast, onto the Daniels.

Part 2: Everywhere (The Daniels) Prior to All At Once I'd never seen a film 'By the Daniels'. I loathe the person who hid these mad genii' from my radar. They are beautifully talented and some of the most creative MF's out there. The directing in this movie is spectacular, pure cinematic joy every single god damn moment. They made a movie that made me die of laughter and then minutes later balling tears of pure emotion. These 2 need to direct a misunderstood comic book character, that's a guaranteed hit, just like attaching Reeves to Batman. I also want to thank them (and A24!) for the beautiful execution of a gay relationship.

Part Three: All At Once (The Movie) Everything Everywhere All At Once is the most meta movie I've ever seen. I don't particularly like meta movies, because the execution is so damn poor and usually all they do is just look right into the camera. This movie has none of that garbage, it has SO many references to different movies and some references to pop culture and even to Michelle Yeoh's previous works, but it is not out of place, it makes sense to be where it is, it's not forced down your throat and it has actual implications to the plot and the multiverse. Speaking of the Multiverse, I've seen several multiverse movie attempts, some are meh and some get pretty cool. The multiverse in this movie is absolute GENIUS. It's not hard to comprehend but is extremely rewarding and complex once you figure everything out. I have a strong belief this will be a better Multiversal mayhem movie than Dr. Strange 2, not to put that movie down whatsoever, it's just the nearest multiverse project.

How well do "you" know the version of yourself (sometimes called "the localized you") with which the majority of us are most familiar? Chances are most of us aren't even aware of any of our other selves, but those well versed in metaphysical circles have a good sense about them, and making audiences aware of this phenomenon is what this manic comedy-drama is all about. When the beleaguered owner of a laundromat is beset by issues with her husband, father, daughter and the IRS, it seems, like the title implies, that everything hits, all at once. But that's nothing compared to what happens when she's unexpectedly contacted by a different version of her spouse who informs her that he's been looking for her for a long time to help resolve an issue with a growing evil in the multiverse, a concept with which she's supposedly best suited but completely unfamiliar. However, as her awareness grows, this new adventure begins opening doors for her in unexpected ways, not only in the universe in which she dwells, but also those in which other versions of herself reside. The result is an insightful and hilarious exploration of some heady philosophical and moral concepts, punctuated by stunningly clever visual effects, huge laughs, clever send-ups of a variety of other films, and dynamite performances by Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Lee Curtis. Nevertheless, despite these assets, the film goes on far too long, telling a story that could have easily been trimmed by about a half-hour, primarily by eliminating some bits that overstay their welcome (such as take-offs of martial arts movies that start out funny but grow tiresome after a few too many runs). This offering from directors Dan Kwan and Daniel Scheinert is certainly an ambitious and inventive release, but it's unfortunate that the filmmakers didn't know when to quit. It's indeed worth a look, but it's regrettable that those responsible for the picture didn't quite know when to stop.

This film is about a lot of things- generational trauma, the immigrant experience, love versus duty, and the choices we make that leave us wondering how our lives could have been if we just said or did that one thing differently. At its core though, I think Everything Everywhere is an argument between absurdism and nihilism; in the face of the meaninglessness of the universe, how should we go about finding meaning in our lives? Should we choose to do so in the first place? I bawled my eyes out but I also laughed, and I left the theater feeling like I'd just had a particularly raw but productive therapy session with the urge to call my mother and recommend this film to everyone I've ever met.

This movie had a lot of fun moments, hilarious insanity, and genuinely poignant themes. Michelle Yeoh feels hand-picked for this role and does an absolutely incredible job in the lead role. The visual style of the movie is entertaining the whole way through and the kept me engaged since there is so much going on and it demanded my attention. My only criticism of the movie is that I enjoyed the first half a lot more because I was having an absolute blast with it. I appreciated the deeper nature and heartfelt moments in the second half, but I feel like when I revisit this film, that first part will be what I look forward to the most. Overall, this is a movie that is inventive in every way imaginable and uses its bizarre premise to tell a genuinely sweet story with deeply human themes.

Everything Everywhere All at Once is a new A24 sci-fi comedy, written and directed by Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, "the Daniels". It stars Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, Stephanie Hsu, and Jamie Lee Curtis. This insane multiverse film has been at the top of a lot of most anticipated lists, myself included. I may not have loved loved loved this one as much as others have, but I thoroughly enjoyed it! I really appreciate how ambitious of a story the Daniels are telling here. I'm a huge fan of their comedic work, writing and directing. However, I felt like from a film such as this, a 2 hour 19 minute runtime was a bit much. Not necessarily a confusing film, just sort of busy.

But the perfect blend of humor and action, apparently Jackie Chan was supposed to be the film's lead, until the Daniels decided to go with a female lead. And I'd say they made the perfect decision. Michelle Yeoh as Evelyn, everything revolves around her dynamic as the mother, wife, and daughter, and she is absolutely amazing in the role! Ke Huy Quan as Waymond in his many takes on the character, phenomenal work. Stephanie Hsu as Joy, Evelyn's daughter, another fantastic performance. Hsu has been doing amazing work recently on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, so I am very happy to see her in this type of unique role. Stunning visual effects and stunt choreography, a lot of impressive stuff to see. This is definitely a niche film, not something I would recommend to everyone. But if you're an A24 fan, or a fan of fun, weird and raunchy, give this one a shot!

Everything Everywhere All at Once, the latest offering from A24, is set to go down as one the most innovative, heartfelt, and nonsensical movies of the year. Starring Michelle Yeoh, the film follows Evelyn Wang, a woman who learns she has the power to exist in parallel universes tasked with stopping the person trying to destroy them all. Evelyn is feeling an increasing amount of pressure as she preps the paperwork for her and her husband's dry cleaning business to go through an audit while also prepping for a Chinese New Year party as well as dealing with her distant daughter. When an alternate version of Waymond appears to tell her the multiverse in trouble and she's the only one who can save it all, Evelyn is swept up in events beyond her control as she finds a way to save everything, everywhere, all at once.

While the premise may sound outlandish (because it is), at the heart of the movie is the generational trauma and interpersonal drama between the Wang family. Evelyn's rejection of her daughter's modern sensibilities, her ever-growing distance from her husband, a looming threat of suicide, and the baggage of any number of past decisions haunt the film from the first frame to the final one. All this is balanced deftly with the sci-fi elements of dimension hopping and universe-spanning adventures. The best science fiction is that which uses the genre trappings to tell a human story and directors Kwan and Scheinert have managed to weave a story that is exactly that. Is the science part of the movie a bit wonky and hand-wavy? Absolutely. But using it to tell the tale of a family on the verge of shattering that is funny, shocking, emotional, and impactful while also finding clever ways to pay homage to classic movies like 2001 and In the Mood for Love makes Everything Everywhere one of the year's best movies.

Michelle Yeoh finally found a vehicle where she could let her talents fly, and fly they do. Without a doubt, Everything Everywhere is firmly her film; all the elements and themes flow through Evelyn Wang and directors Kwan and Scheinert have given her avenues to show both her comedic and dramatic chops. While we've seen these before (think Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon or her role on Star Trek: Discovery), it's rare we get to see such a substantial amount of both at the same time. Her martial arts acumen is well documented; seeing that combined with the dizzying array of other gifts she presents here reminds us that Yeoh has been a consummate performer for three decades and while there isn't a weak link in the acting in this film, no one else is holding a candle to her.

Stephanie Hsu comes pretty close, however. While Yeoh is the film's main focus, Hsu's Joy is handling a lot of the subtle work throughout the film. In a movie that can only be described as ostentatious, Hsu's muted performance makes Joy one of the standout characters. Carrying the brunt of the film's anguish, Hsu is marvelous as she traverses through makeup and costumes as both Joy and the antagonist Jobu Tupaki, the person willing to burn it all down. Hsu and Yeoh's chemistry is electric as the two play off each other, ending in an aching moment of emotional catharsis that is equal parts relief and revelatory. Yeoh and Hsu sell these final moments, the crux of the entire movie, and thanks to their performances, the film rockets from good to great.

Ke Huy Quan, better known to some as Data from the Goonies or Short Round from Indiana Jones, has less to do in the movie than Yeoh or Hsu but is no less important. A main part of the cause of the breaking family that is the Wangs, Quan's Waymond is the paragon of hope and optimism. Contrasted to Evelyn's depressed where-did-it-all-go-wrong mentality, Waymond's ebullience is both infectious and nauseating. While both Evelyn and Joy get multiple opportunities to shine, Waymond gets one great scene with Eveyln towards the end of the film that makes his character's entire trajectory worthwhile. Jamie Lee Curtis appears throughout the film as well as Deirdre, the IRS inspector set to take all that the Wangs hold dear. As a constant antagonist through the film, Curtis is great in her I-could-really-give-a-shit demeanor as a woman who's just doing her job, albeit at the expense of the Wang's livelihood. While the Wangs are the centerpiece of the movie, Curtis manages to compliment them in every scene she's in. James Hong, in less scenes than Curtis, is a delight to see as always as Evelyn's dad and brings a sorely needed gravitas to his scenes that are necessary to keeping the movie anchored.

Directed by The Daniels (Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert), Everything Everywhere is a follow up to their equally inventive Swiss Army Man. Whereas Swiss Army Man presents a more surrealist type of story, Everything Everywhere pushes the envelope even father in terms of inventiveness and creativeness. The main strength of the film, and in The Daniels' storytelling, is the focus on the main issue: a dysfunctional family. Regardless of every bit of nonsense the directors throw at the audience, from our characters portrayed as rocks to a world where everyone has hot dogs for fingers, the story always reverts back to the Wang family and their interconnected struggles. Technically, Everything Everywhere is a masterpiece, managing to consistently shift through genres without losing sight of the objective. Be it the brilliant makeup Hsu's Joy is decked out in or her outlandish costume designs, the level of detail that went into creating the film reveals how well thought out and meticulous The Daniels and their crew are.

Overall, Everything Everywhere All at Once will go down as one of the most impressive displays of creativity and imagination on screen. Daniels Kwan and Scheinert's ability to pull off a zany, darkly comedic sci-fi movie while interweaving a poignant family drama is nothing short of amazing. By far Michelle Yeoh's best role to date (as well as Stephanie Hsu's), Everything Everywhere shines a dazzling spotlight on the actress' myriad talents and specialties. An outrageously inventive premise, combined with strong acting and brilliant direction makes this a phones down, all senses dialed in must watch immediately.

This is a movie you must experience for yourself to fully grasp exactly what it is. I absolutely loved it, and yet I find myself unable to write a coherent review… because the movie is absolutely crazy, as well as being cinematic perfection. It's one of the greatest films I have ever seen, or rather, experienced! Instead of writing a full review, I feel this movie is best described in points, because I don't want to say too much about anything, I just want this to convince anyone reading this to go out and see it as soon as they can (in theatres with an audience)! It's the most original and creative piece of filmmaking I have witnessed in probably the last 5 years, I just can't believe what the directorial duo Daniels was able to pull off here! So without further ado, here are my thoughts on "Everything Everywhere All At Once": 

* The film is flawless and true cinematic perfection in my eyes!
* An assault on the senses; the visuals and sound design are insane!
* Extremely impressive from a technical standpoint. 
    * Editing is a huge standout and was incredibly done, the edit alone took us on a ride! They used match cuts so creatively too!
    * Cinematography was stunning, I especially loved the creative use of lighting!
    * Sound design was absolutely crazy, it had so much going on and complimented the visuals perfectly!
* Every genre of film in one!
* I've never seen anything like it, it's ambitious, crazy, bonkers, insane, creative, hilariously funny, heartfelt, clever, wild, awesome, the best, odd, wacky, touching, chaotic but in a well-written way, stylized, brilliant, and most of all, masterful!
* None of this movie should work, and yet due to the Daniels' excellent and clever direction, it somehow does (and yet I still don't know how they were able to pull it off)
* There is no way Multiverse of Madness will be half as crazy as this movie, this is the best multiverse film we will probably ever see
* The writing so cleverly establishes the multiverse rules and keeps it flowing in a way that allows you to feel like you understand what's going on despite how complex it gets. It perfectly guides you through the story without spoon-feeding it to you, making sure the chaotic multiverse makes sense.
* Also loved the thematic exploration in the story, and that they didn't let the novelty and entertainment value of the multiverse stuff take away from the story, it just complemented it instead. It's some genius writing, especially when heading into the second half of the film where the emotional/thematic core really starts to open up and shine!
* Action is phenomenal and intense. It's some of the best I've seen in the last few years, it's so wild! It's very stylized and impressive, the Daniels know how to direct action so well. They get great coverage that shows off the choreography and every hit, and perfect timing for cuts. 
* The film is so funny, has some witty dialogue, insane gags that I never saw coming, and some hilarious comedic payoffs — one of the funniest movies I've seen in a while, it had both me and the audience howling with laughter!
* Michelle Yeoh's performance is astonishing! She's just awesome as the lead; she's so badass in her action scenes, so funny, and yet still gives such an emotional, heartfelt performance
* I also loved Ke Quan as her husband, he was so loveable and had some of the funniest moments. So great to see him acting again, have really missed him since his days in "Indiana Jones" and "The Goonies".
* Stephanie Hsu was phenomenal as the daughter, and a huge part of why the 2nd half of the film works as well as it does!
* Jamie Lee Curtis had me laughing so hard, she was hilarious here, I've never seen her do anything like this!

We are always surrounded by everything, everywhere all at once and don't even know it 
Michelle Yeoh plays Evelyn, she lives a menial existence working a dead-end job at a laundromat and her life going nowhere 
Her husband is divorcing her and her daughter hates her plus she can't have the heart to tell her father that his granddaughter is gay 
Later one day an inter dimensional rupture unravels reality, she becomes an unlikely hero; turns out she's one of many Evelyns in different universes 
Each have the same face but have different lives and she possesses many of their skills 
Evelyn must channel her newfound powers to fight bizarre and bewildering dangers from the multiverse as the fate of the world hangs in the balance 
The version of over husband is from the Alphaverse whom gas seeked this Evelyn who's much different from many because since she can't do anything she can learn to do everything 
This is very innovative with its visuals and has good family themes 
Michelle Yeoh is a treat to watch jumping into multiple realities 
Each of the relatives has a personal issue with one another 
Yet this is too long and some of it gets very repetitive to the point where it makes no sense 
It's really one of the most bizarre outings I've seen all year assaulting the senses 
A lot of the choices are arbitrary to the point of self indulgent 
But for the Russo Brothers tackling this material it'll be half and half for many as it can be pretty bombastic but also cerebral

Are you looking for a fresh, original take on the Sci-Fi Adventure Comedy genre?  If so, then this film is for you.  Inauspicious Evelyn Wang is struggling with everything in her life.  She's the owner of a flagging laundry business; she's the wife in a lackluster marriage; she's the daughter of a disappointed aging father, and the mother of an alienated daughter.  As a middle-aged and middle generation immigrant from China, Evelyn is stuck between two worlds.  
	Evelyn longs to fulfill unrealized dreams, but each of her many dozens of wishes would require a lifelong dedication to the craft.  She just might be able to experience those lives when a visitor from a parallel universe comes to find her.  The strangely familiar man tells her that she may be the only hope to save the many-verse.  No one in Evelyn's life would have expected her to rise to the challenge, least of all Evelyn herself.
	Everything Everywhere All At Once is incredible.  The plot has all the dramatic import of a hard Sci-Fi film, and the characters take it seriously, but the audience is treated to a delightfully comedic experience throughout.  The film is full of action scenes that deliver expertly choreographed martial art fight sequences.  However, the movie isn't just a vehicle to provide visual fun.  Every part of the plot is interwoven with the relationship between the characters.  Through the view of her other possible lives, Evelyn comes to understand her family more fully than ever before.
	The action, special effects, directing, superb acting, and comedy would be enough for me to recommend this film to anyone.  On top of that, Everything Everywhere All At Once has heart that brought a tear to my eye—a must-watch.

Even after only two movies, I would trust the directing duo Daniels (Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert) with any movie. They have earned a lifetime pass from me. If these men can make the farting corpse of Harry Potter not just one of the weirdest movies of 2016, not just one of the best films of that year, but also one of the most insightful toward the human condition, then these men can do anything. It's been six long years for a follow-up but it sure has been worth it. Everything Everywhere All At Once is, to be pithy, a whole lot of movie. Everything Everywhere (my preferred shorthand from here) is a miracle of a movie. It's a wonder that something this bizarre, this wild, this juvenile, this ambitious, and this specific in vision could find its way through the dream-killing factory that is Hollywood moviemaking. This is the kind of movie you celebrate for simply existing, something so marvelously different but so assured, complex but accessible, and deliriously, amazingly creative. I'm throwing out a lot of adjectives and adverbs to describe the experience of this movie and that's because it filled me with such sheer wonder and divine happiness. I am thankful that the Danirels are making their movies on their terms, and two movies into what I hope is a long and uncompromising career, I can tell that both of these gentlemen deserve all the accolades and plaudits they have coming. I'll try my best not to sound like a simpering moron while I try to explain why this movie is so thoroughly outstanding.

Evelyn (Michelle Yeaoh) is a middle-aged Chinese immigrant who is taking stock of her disappointing life. She and her husband, Waymond (Ke Huy Quan), own a floundering coin-operated laundromat. They're under audit by a dogged IRS agent (Jamie Lee Curtis). Evelyn's disapproving father, Gong Gong (James Hong, still so great even into his 90s), has moved from China to live with the family, and he was never a fan of Waymond, looking down on his daughter for marrying the man. Then there's Joy (Stephanie Hsu), Evelyn and Waymond's twenty-something daughter, who wants to bring her girlfriend to dinner but mom still doesn't accept her daughter's queerness and uses the excuse of Gong Gong's generational disapproval. Then, at the IRS agency, Waymond's body is taken over by another Waymond, Alpha Waymond, who informs Evelyn that she is the key to saving a universe of universes, and she'll have to tap into her alternate selves and their abilities to battle the evil destroyer, Jobu Tupaki, who wants to destroy all existence, and who also happens to be an alternate universe version of Joy.

Multiverses are definitely all the rage right now as they present nostalgic cash-grabs and cameos galore, but Everything Everywhere is a multiverse that is personal and specific. It's based on all the paths the protagonist never took, and each allows her confirmation of what her life could have been, often more glamorous or exciting or initially appealing. A movie star. A famous singer. A ballerina. A skilled chef. Evelyn is a character paralyzed by the disappointment of her life's choices, the malaise that has settled in, and the nagging feeling that things could have and should have been better. In one of the best jokes early on, Evelyn is told she's the Chosen One not because she is special but because she is, literally, living the worst of all possible lives of the multiverse of Evelyns (then again the pinata Evelyn didn't look like an upgrade). She has taken all the many bad paths and dead ends, but this positions her as the only one who has the power to tap into every other power and ability from her multiverse duplicates. It's one thing to be feeling like you should have made a different choice in the past, and it's another to get confirmation. This backhanded revelation could just serve as its own joke but it actually transforms into a philosophy that coalesces in the final act, that of all the universes and possibilities we could have had, the best one is the one we are actually present for. In another universe, one very much styled like In the Mood for Love, where a Waymond who was rejected by Evelyn long ago reconnects with her, mournful of what could have been, and says, "In another life, I would have really liked doing laundry and taxes with you," in reference to Evelyn's dismissive summation of what his unrequited romantic "what if" would have lead to. It's such a poignant moment. By the end of the movie, it's become a journey of self-actualization but tied to self-acceptance, where kindness and empathy are the real super weapons and the answer to the tumult of postmodern nihilism.

Smartly, the Daniels have made sure that a universe-hopping threat is actually connected to our hero in a meaningful manner. By making the villain an alternate version of Joy, it raises the stakes and forces Evelyn to have to confront her own parenting miscues and frayed relationship with her daughter. It's the kind of decision-making that reinforces the emotional and thematic core of a movie that is spinning so fast that it feels like you might fall off and vomit new colors. Joy is an avatar of generational disconnect, inherited disappointment and resentment, but what really makes her relatable is the growing feeling of being over it all. Given the power to see everything in every universe, Joy concludes that life is overwhelming and without meaning. It's the same sort of nihilism we might feel today as we doom scroll through our phones, eyes glazed over from the barrage of bad news, outraged click bait, and feeling of abject helplessness while the world spins on in an uncertain direction. It's not hard to feel, as Joy, that it's all too much to bear, and if she can experience everything then does it present value to anything? If she can always just sidestep to another universe, what does that do to the value of life? That's the ethical conundrum with Rick and Morty, a show where they can swap characters from other dimensions to fix more costly mistakes. What Daniels attempts with Everything Everywhere is to tackle the same question but approaching a different answer: that despite everything, life matters, our relationships matter, and kindness and empathy matter most. Watching Evelyn and Joy, and their many different versions of mother and daughter, try to reach an understanding, it's easy to feel that struggle and relate to wanting to feel seen. As Evelyn encouragingly says to one character at their lowest point, "It is too much to handle, yes. But nobody is ever alone."

This is a dozen different kinds of movies, all smashed together, and each of them is utterly delightful and skillfully realized and executed. If you like martial arts action, there are some excellent fight sequences including a showstopper where Waymond wrecks a team of security guards with a fanny pack. The action is exciting and the martial arts choreography is impressive and filmed in a pleasing style that allows us to really appreciate the moves and countermoves. If you like wild comedies, there are many outlandish moments that combine low-humor and highbrow references. I'll simply refer to one as finding payoffs for IRS auditor trophies shaped like butt plugs. This is one of the funniest American comedies in years. If you like family dramas, there is plenty of conflict across the board between Evelyn and Waymond and Joy, plus the specter of Gong Gong, and each person trying to communicate their dissatisfaction and desires for a better life. If you removed all of the crazy sci-fi elements, googly eyes, people's heads turning to confetti, and what have you, this would still be a compelling human drama. When the movie isn't working through ridiculous tangents, or eye-popping action, or a staggering combination of kitsch and intelligence, it's building out its emotional core, the heart of the movie, the thing that makes all the gee-whiz fun matter, the family in flux. Likewise, this is a powerfully optimistic movie, life-affirming in all the best ways without being pandering, and one that is without any flash of ironic condescension. Sincerity is powerful and all over.

The movie is elevated even higher by the strength of the performances. Yeoh (Crazy Rich Asians) has spent decades as a martial arts master, and of late she's been branching out in more demanding dramas, but this is easily the finest performance of her career for nothing less than playing a dozen different characters. She is sensational. The early Evelyn is full of despair and regret, and as she gets to explore each new version of herself, there's an excitement that's bristling, as she gets to see the successes she could have been and celebrate. Yeaoh is hilarious and deeply affecting in the central role and still very much a badass. She showcases starting range, it makes you weep that she has never gotten to play so many different kinds of roles because she's so good at all of them. Hsu (The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel) is the wounded soul, and her sneers and seen-it-all attitude are killer without losing track of the pain at the core of the character. Her emotional confrontations with her mother still hit hard. But the secret weapon of this movie is Quan, the former child actor best remembered as playing Data in The Goonies and Short Round in Temple of Doom. Yes, that same actor. He too gets to play such a wide, wild variety of Waymonds, from the doting and meek husband, to the confidant warriors, to the smoldering former flame, but with each new Waymond, Quan makes you fall in love with the original more. The character of Waymond and his central philosophy of kindness is so moving and needed, that we almost get to fall in love and re-evaluate this man the same way Evelyn does. Also of note, Curtis (Knives Out) is having an absolute blast as her menacing IRS agent.

It's truly amazing to me that a movie can have some of the silliest, craziest, dumbest humor imaginable, and then find ways to tie it back thematically and make it yet another important thread that intricately ties into the overall impact of the movie. The genius of Daniels is marrying the most insane ideas with genuine pathos. Take for instance that one of the many multiverses involves people with hot dogs instead of fingers. It's a goofy visual, and it could simply have been that, a passing moment to make you smile, but the Daniels don't stop there. They continue developing their ideas, all of their ideas, and find additional jokes and purposes few could. Okay, so this is a big divergence from history, so how could humans evolve to have hot dogs for fingers? Well the movie actually showcases this moment in a hilarious 2001: A Space Odyssey reference. And then the film says, "Well, if this was the way of life, what other practices would evolve from here when it comes to communication and intimacy?" It's that level of development and commitment that blows me away. The same with what starts as Evelyn's misunderstanding of the Pixar movie Ratatouille. It works just as a joke in the moment, but then it comes back as its own reality, and even that reality has a thematic resonance by the end. This level of imagination, to take the weirdest jokes and make them meaningful, is special. In one second, I can cry laughing from a raccoon and in the next second a rock can make me want to cry. In essence, even though Everything Everywhere is beyond stuffed, nothing is merely disposable.

That doesn't mean that the film doesn't also fall victim to repetition at points. My only criticism, and it might even be eliminated entirely after a second viewing, is that Daniels can over indulge when it comes to their narrative points. Some things can get stretched out, so that they hit points with five beats when three could have been sufficient. It's this kind of mentality that pushes the running time to almost two hours and twenty minutes, which feels a bit extended. However, the messiness and overstuffed nature of the movie is also one of its hallmarks, so I don't know if this criticism will even register for many, especially if you're fully on board their wacky wavelength.

If you can, please go into Everything Everywhere All At Once knowing as little as possible. The carousel of surprise and amazement is constant, but the fact that there is a strong emotional core, that all the many stray elements become perfectly braided together, no matter how ridiculous, is all the more impressive. This is stylized filmmaking that is very personal while also being accessible and universal in its existential pains and longing. It's style and substance and exhilarating and genius and emotionally cathartic and moving and everything we want with movies. It's the kind of movie that reignites your passion for cinema, the kind that delivers something new from the studio system, and the kind that deserves parades in celebration. Simply put, as I said before, this is a miracle of a movie, and you owe it to yourself to feel this blessing.

90/100 Supremely imaginative and ambitious, the film, if nothing else, is a triumph of creativity. It manages to be suspenseful, action packed, laugh-out loud funny, throughly absurd, and at times, genuinely moving and heartfelt. Throughout much of the runtime, it succeeds at stacking its many tones together in a way that, rather than producing tonal confusion, achieves a coherent, multi-faceted product. Given the far-reaching amalgamation that "Everything, Everywhere, All At Once" simply is, it's amazing that it works, and works beautifully. It shouldn't, but it simply does. Oh, and did I mention style...? This film has style upon style upon style--It's practically dripping in style. At once macro and micro, it tucks a grandiose cosmic narrative into a grounded human drama. It does so, not because the filmmakers have stumbled upon some new idea, but because the ordinary drama of human life is inherently wondrous. However, for all its successes, the film's final philosophical conclusion does not succeed as well as intended. The main antagonist is a personification of existential dread. Or, more specifically, one might say, "depressive nihilism". And, while the film makes strides to combat this enemy through love, kindness, and the revelation that locates the good life, not in the life you could have had, but in the relationships (however imperfect they are) and the redemption of such relationships that one has at present, it does so, not through a recovery of transcendent meaning, but through a gleeful nihilism; a positive spin on the meaninglessness of everything. For the main characters, this means that they no longer have to shoulder the unbearable weight of trying and failing to make their life all they yearn for it to be. They are, in a sense, liberated to focus on the relationships they've been blessed with, finding meaning and joy in them, rather than in some other imagined or desired life. The message is powerful and right, but the method is faulty. After all, if one arrives at such a conclusion through a dismissal of all meaning, rather than the particular dismissal of certain counterfeit meanings, it begs the question: what then is meaningful about the the character's newfound meaning in life? In this philosophical context, it too must be meaningless, which robs the characters (and the audience) of anything good they think they've found, rendering it a mirage in the dessert. Admittedly, the film is consciously absurd, and appeals to traditional logic may appear irrelevant due to its dedication to illogic; reason's inverted image. And yet, the excellence of the film-making and the writer's attempt to make sense of the senseless both betray whatever absurdist rhetoric the film attempts to spread around. In the end, while the film boasts meaninglessness, the deeper transmission gives a counter testimony; one that declares form, beauty, and meaning. It cannot help itself from preaching such, and while it is a frustrating contradiction, it is perhaps an appropriate irony. Through its conclusion, the film shows its true imaginative limits; limits set by the scope of modern philosophical sensibilities unable to stand firmly in any transcendent meaning whatsoever. For a film so wonderfully cosmic, at the end of the day, the cosmos in which it occurs remains decidedly empty by its own arguments. That said, there is a limit to the extent to which my conceptual grievance subtracts from what is otherwise a nearly perfect film. 4.5/5 stars!

My brain felt like it was stretched to the point my consciousness traveled completely across different multiverses and then being absolutely slingshotted back together to then melt and then blossom into a butterfly. Does that even make sense?! I DON’T EVEN KNOW! But I feel like my IQ Level has increased while watching this film. Michelle Yeoh as Evelyn Wang carrys this film! With an astounding performance. But let me tell you this! Ke Huy Quan steals the movie as Waymond Wang! The acting by this man is sensational! Stephanie Hsu as Joy Wang is good in this. Especially channeling multiple emotions all at the same time! This cast was amazing. And the action is full on entertaining! This movie is split into parts! Part 1 is so good! But Part 2 for me just falls flat in the middle for me. Especially for a scene that dragged on for way too long. To a point a couple people in my theater flat out left. But the end to Part 2 and Part 3 is such a damn good conclusion it makes up for some of the pacing issues this movie has in Part 2. But I will give this movie props on how funny and emotional it truly is. Overall this movie won’t be for everyone! But if you can trust the journey this film has and stick with it through all of its absolutely insane, wacky, mind bending extravaganza. Not only is this easily the finest cinema experience I've seen so far from 2022, I highly doubt I'll see anything to match it by December 31st, let alone surpass it. The Oscar for production design should already have Jason Kisvardy's name on it, but every award 'Dune' was at this year's awards should go to 'Everything Everywhere At at Once', and then some. That should also go for set decoration & art direction, editing, cinematography, writing, and directing...and then some.
And every acting award Michelle Yeoh is eligible for should have her name on them well before they're handed out. She is a powerhouse but also gives a seminar on basically every element of acting, from straight action hero to romantic lead to the subtle expression of love for one's child...and then some. 
The film touches on philosophic points and ideas of how we are constantly caught up in the tedious, the bureaucratic, the chaotic and stressful, the minutiae and the 'big issues' without being a lecture or taking any sides socio-politically or really even culturally. We're all guilty victims, hurting and being hurt while just trying to tread water among the waves of pressure and expectation. All these forces pull us away from one another, but they also build up and cause us to take it out on one another in too often traumatic ways.
The roiled turmoil goes on and on, but it gets us to where Evelyn is with Joy at the end. It gets us to when she tells her father who Becky really is to Joy. It gets us to the IRS auditor Deirdre Beaubeirdra's (Jamie Lee Curtis for Best Supporting!) kindness. 
The scene on the rock planet knocked me out, bringing everything down to the simplest, most basic state of being, in a sense, where we see so clearly all the absurdities of the rest of the universes we see in endless clashes. 
Just spellbinding work by directors and writers Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert. And so much thanks for the work of those in smaller roles here, but especially to the other principal actors Stephanie Hsu, Ke Huy Quan and James Hong.

Get your own multiverse.  So this is about a laundromat owner (Michelle Yeoh).  She is currently being audited by the IRS, but will soon find bigger fish to fry when she is tasked with saving the multiverse by inter-dimensionally hopping psyches of different versions of herself in more ways than you can imagine.  Now, this is one that I was very much anticipating.  The trailers looked crazy in the best way possible, and if you think the multiverse hopping in No Way Home was a lot, well I hope you saved room for dessert.  Everything Everywhere All at Once has been getting rave reviews, and while I may not be as gung-ho as the majority, there's still a whole lot to love about the film they put together.  This movie has quite a few positives going for it, and I completely understand the rave response it has been receiving.  I feel like the most apropos comparison I can make is that this is like straight-faced Rick and Morty.  That's not to say there aren't jokes.  This is laugh-out-loud funny at several different points, but it appeals to that same demographic without being so cynical.  The character setup is fast but effective, and you learn everything you need to know about who these people are in a very condensed period of time.  I also think the performances of Michelle Yeoh and Ke Huy Quan deserve a lot of praise, the latter of which plays her husband.  They have to go back and forth between playing the same characters in different dimensions, and it gets quite nuanced.  Quan, in particular, has to showcase a large range going between nebbish and alpha male, and it is funny every single time he switches between the two.  Everything I've described so far sounds stupendous, so why am I not quite drinking the Kool-Aid with everyone else?  I wanted to like this even more than I did because the creativity that went into this is as plain as the nose on your face.  There is a lot of randomness that gets injected into any given scene, and it sometimes leads to a big laugh.  At other times, it overstays its welcome by returning to the same gag with diminishing returns.  I'll keep it vague so as to avoid spoilers, so I will just say that I felt that the universe involving a hot dog similarity did not need to be revisited so many times.  That leads me directly to my other critique: there is no reason for this to clock in at 140 minutes.  You can cut this down to two hours easily, and it would have a tighter flow and a much larger rewatchability factor.  Personal feelings aside, I have to urge that you seek this out for yourself because the potential for this to be your new favorite movie is very real.

Directing duo Daniel Scheinert and Daniel Kwan's sci-fi family drama Everything Everywhere All At Once (2022) is a mind blowing experience that takes filmmaking to the next level. Daniels' direction is simply marvelous as they take the ambitious and experimental nature of arthouse and student films with the heartfelt nature of an indie drama with a technical mastery of more seasoned directors. Cinematographer Larkin Seiple must be a genius like Daniels as every close-up shot is jaw-dropping. Seiple's precision for every one of his sweeping wide shots make fights roar to life and each conversation feels like the only thing happening in the world. I cannot understand how Daniels' even shot Everything Everywhere All At Once. It truly is one of the most creative pictures ever crafted with a honed precision and dreamy imagination.

Michelle Yeoh is simply enchanting in Everything Everywhere All At Once. Yeoh is phenomenal as stressed heroine Evelyn Wang with her deft martial arts skills and sincerely moving dramatic performance over her marital, life, financial, and parental anxieties. Her gentle expressions of regret and unhappiness are very subtle with an impressive sense of belonging to her family. Yeoh really captures Evelyn's strong spirit of juggling an astute businesswoman, caring wife, protective mother, and supportive woman with her role that I'm sure will ring true for all the ladies in the audience. She's empowered in how complex and messy her life feels. 

I found Yeoh to be so natural and funny for all of Daniels' erratic jokes for Evelyn. She's astounding during every martial arts combat sequence as if she were still in Supercop, Tai Chi Master, or Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. I hope Michelle Yeoh is up for Best Actress at The Oscars as she delivers a versatile and nuanced acting display like few, if any, other actresses could even perform. Michelle Yeoh is absolutely cool, incredibly subtle, totally devastating, and surprisingly funny as Everything Everywhere All At Once's lead actress.

Ke Huy Quan remains hilarious as he was in Temple of Doom and The Goonies with his endearing hero Waymond Wang. I cannot believe he still speaks with that soft and squeaky voice that's so funny for his comedic delivery. He pulls off goofy husbandry and suave romance with equal grace, not to mention his stunning action choreography. I had no idea he could dish out serious martial arts like he does here with a fanny pack and sheer determination. I'm certain every viewer will love and adore Ke Huy Quan's Waymond. 

Stephanie Hsu is brilliant as Evelyn's often ignored daughter Joy Wang. You feel her conflicted feelings of devotion to her mother and family, while wanting to be accepted as her true lesbian self. Hsu is charming, funny, and moving as Joy. I found her alternate villainess Jobu Tupacki a killer addition like an antagonist out of Legion. She's all very pretty with a striking face and absorbing eyes. James Hong is hilarious and gripping as always with his delightful stubborn grandfather Gong Gong. Jamie Lee Curtis steps outside her comfort zone to play a blunt and impatient IRS auditor Deirdre Beaubeirdra. She gets to have neat fights with Michelle Yeoh and brings a strange humor to all her scenes. Tallie Medel is very charming and pretty as Joy's girlfriend Becky Sregor with her having to deal with awkward situations with grace.

Harry Shum Jr.'s Chad and Jenny Slate's dog totting Big Nose are so funny. There's a ton of other delightful cameos here. All of the stunt fighters are really outstanding with unreal combat skills as they bravely face off against Michelle Yeoh herself. Randy Newman somehow got cast as the gruff voice of Raccacoonie.

Everything Everywhere All At Once feels like there were thousands of scenes shot for quick moments and deep emotional connections. Editor Paul Rogers does the impossible by splicing together hundreds upon hundreds of scenes with rapid fire montages and hard jump cuts to entirely new worlds while keeping Daniels' story coherent that you can still follow. Rogers' sharp editing keeps Everything Everywhere All At Once into a fast paced 139 minutes that feels like a half hour.

I am incredibly impressed with how Daniels' effortlessly blends the earnest family drama of films like The Farewell and CODA with stunning tender romance of In the Mood for Love and the social commentary of Parasite. Daniels' provides action choreography straight out of Supercop, John Wick, The Raid, or Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. I cannot believe that stylistically Daniels' direction feels inspired by mind bending art films like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind or a crafty television series like Legion. There's even a multiverse like Spider-Man: No Way Home! It's easy to see what producers Joe and Anthony Russo saw in Daniels as directors. Everything Everywhere All At Once is clearly the greatest film of the year! See it on the silver screen in theaters as soon as you can!

Writers Daniel Scheinert and Daniel Kwan deliver a really heartfelt family drama at the heart of Everything Everywhere All At Once. You get a family struggling to pay bills and expand their laundromat business because they're getting their taxes audited by the IRS all while balancing a strained marriage and their lesbian daughter's new relationship. Daniels brings a character focused story to deeply moving conclusions about being satisfied with your lot in life, finding joy in your family and love life, let alone their life affirming message that nothing really matters, so just have fun with life. 

It never lingers on the nihilism and instead embraces quirky meta humor, intimate romance, and thoughtful parenting advice with an ultimately hopeful message. I honestly felt inspired after seeing Everything Everywhere All At Once to be more spontaneous and playful and take everything in life in stride. We could all use a reassuring realization that life is what you make of it, so take it easy on yourself and appreciate your loved ones and daily experiences. Daniels' script has hilarious jokes, devastating drama, outrageous irreverence, breathtaking beauty, enthralling action sequences, and a genius structure for their unbelievable story.

Jason Kisvarday's production design creates a cozy home and quaint laundromat alongside a sterile IRS office for all the absurd events of Everything Everywhere All At Once. I love how sets shift around and feel so specific to each area. Amelia Brooke's art direction has a uniquely comforting look and feel to the home spaces, while everywhere else is surreal with a sci-fi twist. Set decorators Kelsi Ephraim, Madelyn Wilkime, Hunter Gorton, Lia Burton, Sierra Harbison, Ian Lapidus, and Anne Stericker stuff the homes with furnishings and props galore to gaze at just like the IRS office has props to fight with as weapons. I have no concept of how visual effects artists Evan Halleck, Matthew Wauhkonen, Zak Stoltz, Ethan Feldbau, Jeff Desom, and Benjamin Brewer pull off all the CGI. But it really looks realistic and grounded no matter how insane the narrative evolves.

Composer Son Lux crafts a pulsing electronic post-rock score that really suits Everything Everywhere All At Once's chaotic atmosphere. I loved when the bass really became grainy and hectic during a huge plot reveal or thrilling combat. Son Lux' beautiful melodies fit the gentle romantic moments as well with a serene vibe and pleasant sound. Sound designers Kailand C. Reilly, Andrew Twite, Brent Kiser, Ian Chase, Jacob Flack, and Alexandra Fehrman mix all manner of noises from characters screaming into battle to black hole bagels being opened up in the world.

Costume designers Shirley Kurata, Courtney Hess, Lisa Russey, Kristina Selby, Andrea Tsanas, and Alex Woehrle legitimately appear to have woven hundreds of dresses and outfits for Michelle Yeoh alone, not to mention Stephanie Hsu's sci-fi fits that look so fresh on her. I cannot believe they really made entire costumes for split second scenes. Make-up artists Dania Simental, Michelle Chung, Christine Choi, and Abigail Bradley ensure Michelle Yeoh and Stephanie Hsu are drop dead gorgeous in every scene with a pleasant variety of aesthetics. From the grounded poverty to space chic and everything in between is represented here.

In the end, Everything Everywhere All At Once is a touching indie drama I adored and found myself tearing up during, despite the film also being brain pounding sensory annihilation.

I have watched this amazing film in the theatre three times so far, and I finally decided to register on Rotten Tomato to leave some of my thoughts. For those of you who have not seen it yet, it is a bonkers cinema experience that you deserve to at least give a try without knowing much about it. I believe most people will not regret it!

My Thoughts (LIGHT SPOILERS CONTAINED)

1. It is an edgy and bonkers cinema experience deliberated crafted as it is - the theme of the movie is literally about everything of life, and you supposed to love and hate some parts of it. So I totally understand those 1-star reviewers who hate this movie, and I guess I am just lucky to be the ones who loves the movie very much.

2. The representation of Asian immigrant family is on point - I doubt there will be other groups of people who ask themselves "what ifs" more often from time to time. It is never easy to make life-changing decisions to leave at least part of your family to embark a journey of unknown in a foreign land. The distance from their own culture, the conflicts with the new ones, and the learnings and evolvements over time are shaping them to be unique group of people that are their own kind. Being children of Asian American family is like trapped in between, where you are raised with family of tradition value while attempted by the free thoughts from the outside world - it is essential a struggle between collectivism and individualism. In some cases, I guess the intergenerational trauma is inevitable. 

3. Oh I love the PHILOSOPHY discussed in the film - I was once fallen to the idea of nihilism as I discovered that science could not essentially prove "objective truth", instead, it could only present you with the theories that are not disapproved yet. So by definition, everything we know could be false, even though we human beings may never have the ability to tell anyways. It left me with such a feeling of emptiness and meaninglessness - what is the point to believe in anything if nothing matters? I found some relief later in the existentialism, as I am glad to have this may-be-fake right to choose what I believe, that gives you a break while providing you with a tiny sense of being human. I chose kindness and hope because I like them, and I wish them to be true.

4. Is this film perfect? Surely nothing in life is perfect, and I guess it is one of the lessons you take from this movie as well. Do I believe the movie could be shorter and concise in some parts, and tighten up things faster in the ending parts? Maybe. But it  simply DOES NOT MATTER as I appreciate the movie as a whole and the full package it presented. Also, why does it matter anyways as I am only one of the many small piece of shits who have opinions. Just be a rock and appreciate what you have in your life.

Everything Everywhere All At Once is a truly dazzling film, an assault on the senses, a feast for the eyes. Original and unique, it's quite a glorious cinematic experience. It's hard to categorise and probably hard to define and explain but this wild and crazy sci-fi romp is one of the most unique experinces you will possibly have in years. It starts simply as we find Evelyn Wang trying to run a struggling laundromat. Her father has just arrived from China and her husband is trying to divorce her. but it escalates when she needs to visit the IRS office to sort out her tax audit. It is here that the film gets tunred upside down. We enter a world of multi personalities and multi verses. Her husband informs Evelyn that she needs to navigate the multiverses to stop all of them being destroyed. What ensues is a chaotic ride of martial arts and dazzling action scenes. There is sense to be made of it but also no sense. You need to suspend your logic and just hang on for the ride. It's non stop action and at times it becomes a bit too much. But at a certain point in the film it gels together and the action slows and we experience a film that is more about family conenctions and regret of lives lived. It somehow manages to become not just a sublime action film but one is also emotionally powerful. Michelle Yeoh is truly superb as Evelyn and she carries the film majestically. This sensory overload film is best on the big screen. Just sit in the dark and let yourself sink in.

Undeniably one of the most whacked out, imaginative, convention-busting movies I've seen in a long, long time and quite possibly my favorite within the A24 catalog to date, "Everything Everywhere All At Once" finds co-writers/co-directors Dan Kwan and Daniel Scheinert harnessing that signature blend of humor and emotionality that Sundance audiences fell in love with back in 2016 and channeling it through some of the most brilliantly creative subject matter you can get in media today. The balancing of tones, storylines, plants and payoffs — it's like watching a high-wire act involving the juggling of both chainsaws and puppies at the same time. Daniels, however, end up excelling in nearly every intangible facet. Aside from a couple structural issues that I had towards the end of the film, this is an emotionally satisfying, superbly realized adventure, with resonant thematics and some gut-busting laughs. Hoping the duo at hand has many, many more projects like this in the works.

I am apparently joining the choir here by saying that I heard this was a great movie, went into it with nervously high expectations and yet wasn't disappointed at all. They made tremendous, inspiring use of mundane settings where it felt very much like rather than construct a set they had taken a real laundromat and office building and made some serious movie magic in there. When they started explaining the premise by interrupting the IRS meeting it was so frantic that I thought their explanation was gonna be too brief for me to fully understand it, but they actually did a great job with it and hit a perfect balance of coherence and pacing. The minor details really sealed the deal in making this an instant classic -- the blood splatter hitting the camera, the egg on the lady's shirt, the correct wrestling terminology, the semi-subtle Nine Days song reference, etc. The score wasn't grand but they used it very effectively to alter the mood. Waymond reminded me of Data so much that this almost felt like a very loose Goonies spinoff, in a good way. I will say that the transition from part 1 to part 2 was mildly exasperating in that a whole lot of movie had happened by that point and the pace slowed to such a degree that the conclusion feel a bit drawn out, and they went a little too heavy on the hotdog fingers when there were funnier jokes to choose from, but those are relatively small knocks on what is otherwise just a complete masterpiece. Everything Everywhere All At One - 10/10. Daniels (Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert) direct this incredibly crafted multi genre film that is extremely hard to describe. But here's a try. A mother whose family is in tax trouble is thrust into a multiverse dilemma which sees her having to fight against her daughter and many other foes in multiple different timelines. Whilst this happens, she goes through the philosophical and metaphysical ringer, changing the way she views her life and her overall world view. Also, she learns the true meaning of life: being and living with kindness. Packed with full throttle action, hilariously outrageous comedy, and deep looks at the meaning of many things, this movie is literally a life changing experience. I don't usually get affected by many movies. But this film is an experience altogether. Its so incredibly entertaining in so many different ways. It will make you laugh, make you cry, make you think, and change the way you view life. Its introspective, but also looks at the deeper meaning of life. Michelle Yeoh delivers a career defining performance. She always delivers in action, but we see her full scope of her acting abilities in this. Ke Huy Quan and Stephanie Hsu deliver solid performances as well, along with a hilarious villainous performance from Jamie Lee Curtis. But I just love the overall message of this film. Its a much needed message, and one that really speaks to the human experience. A full experience that you must see in theatres! The best film of the year so far!

The only thing that gave me pause was the casual antisemitism of calling the one Jewish character and actress "Big Nose." People audibly gasped in the theater. Is this ok in 2022? Antisemitic hate crimes are on the rise globally, and Jewish people are the targets of over 60% of all hate crimes in the United States alone, despite making up only 1.5% of the population. I could see that it was a flaw of Evelyn's character, as she was judgmental in other ways about other people. But unlike those other comments, this was never addressed again, and the character was never given another name--it was left as "Big Nose" in the credits. I have to assume Jenny Slate was ok with it, but as a Jewish person sitting in the audience, I was immediately anxious and uncomfortable. It sucks to have to write that about a movie that I would now easily regard as one of the most beautiful films I have ever seen, and I can't excuse or explain away that part.

This collage of entertaining moments is no doubt a dazzling accomplishment, but does it have beauty? A petri dish of egalitarian ecstasy, where your everyday American immigrant family doubles (&triples ad infinitum) as multiverse superheroes, destined to destroy all life or save it. Destroy it because of the seeming pointlessness of it all (the Nihilistic winner) or save it with the hands of maternal love (existentialist winner). For the quick fix youtube videogamer types, these paltry deeper themes are nothing but the context for the eye and ear candy, which the Daniels so deliciously serve up. And for the cineastes, they may prefer the Coen's strain of California nihilism in The Big Lewbowki. And for others, I Heart Huckabees may satisfy your exploration into the meaning and underpinning of the universe. But if you head to the cinema to observe EEAAO, you can't help but be drawn in towards the pretty pictures, or at the minimum have your eyes and ears splashed with the meteoric stimulation crashing into you. With the hi jinks of a Michele Gondry film, the adrenaline of a marvel movie and the story of a B action movie, it amount to a lot - or does it? Yes, it cuts deeper than a B action flick because we are talking about the cosmos, the universe and the meaning of life, but ultimately the film functions as a series of scenes digressing from that central spine. So that discursive narrative never packs the emotional punch many crave from the cinema. It's a not a rich satisfying meal in that way. Instead, it's a technological achievement of craft and a deft, playful and expansive exploration of the power of visual storytelling. Leaning into the visual, less on the story. The Daniel's hit a home run and whatever our taste may be that's deserving of applause. Will the film be dismissed if it doesn't take home the trophies at the end of the season, it doesn't matter. Don't get too caught up in the philosophic or sophomoric, and you'll be just where you're meant to be: ready to enjoy.

I oscillated between 4.5 and 5 stars, but I'm going to throw 5 down as a long-term prediction because I'm sure on rewatch I'll be able to pick up on and appreciate even more without losing an ounce of enjoyment around the belly-laugh comedy, clever action, and infectious filmmaking passion that can be found at every turn in this film. It scales up the simple life lesson of appreciate WHO you have in your life to multiversal proportions, at once giving us a wickedly entertaining rendition of this theme and a consistent yet fresh reinforcement of this theme many times over in this single story. The performances from Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan (a revelation in this), and Jamie Lee Curtis were fantastic with their dynamic portrayals of various versions of their characters. The Daniels' ability to take philosophical ideas and ground them in quirky situations and silly metaphors (the "Everything Bagel" black hole as the face of nihilism, so good) again adds to the simple yet profound nature of this film. The critiques that nearly held me back were that the older guy's arc seemed less genuine and more plot-determined, the cross-cutting toward the end to emphasize the message sort of undercut the emotional dimension to the main conversation between Evelyn and Joy, and the film can almost be an overload with how much is going on both visually and within the narrative. However, to be 5 stars a film need not be perfect. It must have substantive themes that are well-realized through the characters, it must draw out a strong emotional reaction (being brought to the verge of tears through sadness and through laughter suffices, as does a pumping heart from thick tension; a strong intellectual response, i.e. thinking about it a lot after seeing it, does so too), and it must craft a vivid atmosphere that offers a distinct originality to its exploration of a premise. This film doesn't just check those boxes, it puts googly eyes on them. [REWATCH UPDATE]: Oh yes, full 5 for sure. Loved it even more. The scene of Evelyn and Waymond reconnecting, with glimpses of all his overflowing joy and silliness intercut between the colorful light dancing on each of their faces, that struck the soul. And the crosscutting with the other multiverses later in the climax weren't meant to strike that same emotional tone, they were meant to showcase the various facets of life, where a deeply intimate conversation on a green-tinted Chinese street is just as meaningful and full of humanity as dancing around with hot dog fingers or offering to lift someone on your shoulders so you can reunite them with their racoon. As for the Gong Gong storyline, it also became more clear to me what the message there was. He easily let Evelyn go because she did not fit into his expectations/wishes for her (when she leaves to America), and Alpha Gong Gong does the same thing in trying to kill this version of his daughter in order to stop the risk of her joining Jobu. However, Alpha Gong Gong comes around to Evelyn trying to save her daughter (refusing to "let her go" into the bagel) and real Gong Gong doesn't disavow the family or Becky once he finds out Joy has a girlfriend, implying that he's able to accept the messiness of his family that doesn't live up to those ideal expectations he has. Again, it's not as strong as the others because it is less developed, but it still works, and most importantly it is a big milestone in Evelyn's arc--she no longer is ashamed to be honest with her father about her life because his disapproval won't shatter her. Other ideas the film explores also came through and landed better this time; Waymond's philosophy of being kind and cheery as a necessary strategy to navigate the cruel work is so wonderfully shown AND articulated in the film, and the line "in another life, I'd be happy just doing laundry and taxes with you" is lovely. The optimistic angle of the film isn't a complete negation of nihilism, it's an embrace of absurdism. I missed Evelyn's "we can do whatever we want...nothing matters" in her talk with Joy the first time around. The film still poses the idea that, sure, nothing matters and we're insignificant little humans running around without a clue of what to do, but that means we can choose to invest time into what we care about and to make those things matter in our lives because we give them meaning. That is Albert Camus' absurdism 101. So once again, great film. Only lingering question is why Joy ran from Evelyn when she announced Becky as her girlfriend; didn't she want that early in the film, and didn't she want a connection with her mother (shown by Evelyn's speech of 'me and my daughter are alike')? The thing I'm thinking is the way Evelyn expressed that connection was saying we're alike and then deprecating herself a lot, so making Joy feel bad? I don't know, it seemed like the script NEEDED Joy to run off so we could have one final conversation (which I thought was effective, of course), but I'm not sure why on the character level Joy responded SO negatively. Why was that the breaking point? But regardless, this film is a gem. Should have been the biggest hit of this year. It's everything you can want out of a film: it's interesting, it's entertaining, it's thought-provoking, and it's moving. It is a masterpiece.

The film is full of bright colors and ridiculous costumes. Individually, there are moments where people are individually attempting to shove things up their butts in an action sequence, a puppet raccoon controls a Benihana chef a la Ratatouille, and ... a woman attempts to reconcile her own life choices and disillusionment with her difficult relationship with her own daughter, including elements of culture clash intergenerational change. And yet it all comes together with such vibrancy, entertainment value, and emotional power. An incredible balance between character development and irreverent humor in a successful attempt to establish a unique existentialist flavor. There's something for everyone here.

Liking this movie depends on how you feel about its core message.  I found it saccharine and phony.  

The trailer states in a somber tone, "the multiverse depends on you" but really, it's just a story about a family.  The metaphor might have worked if the movie didn't get so silly.  The daughter is depressed and represents the un-glorious path of her mother who could have been so much more if it wasn't for her and her nice-guy-finishes-last husband.  The main character can see all of the lives she has lived in the multiverse; the one she lives in is the one where she made "all the wrong choices".  She owns two small businesses, is married and has a daughter; only in Hollywood is that considered the worst of all worlds.  Therein lies the conceit; she lives a normal, and by historical standards a blessed life with the disappointments we all face but the movie makes out that it is much worse than it is.

Like a bad sit-com, it all gets tied up in the end with a phony message; "no matter what happens, if I did it with you, I wouldn't change it for anything".  What drivel.

It's also scattered and too long.  The most recent Spider-Man movie is a much better multiverse movie, and more emotionally genuine.

There are so many words that one could use to describe this film. The one that immediately comes to mind is "unexpected". The trailer initially struck me as belying a masterpiece, a diamond in the rough. In a sea of superhero laden multi movie deals and gritty reboot pocked release windows, Everything Everywhere All At  distinguishes itself by telling a very human story with an ultimate sense of finality and satisfaction. Without spoiling anything, the film follows Michelle Yeoh and crew on a journey to find acceptance and love in a multiverse seemingly gone mad. The plot is excellently developed from the first scene and does not miss a beat. You'll be on edge till the credits roll. A few tender moments are sprinkled in for effect. The effects and paraphernalia laden choreography are truly on a level never before scene in film. Fans of the classic 80s Hong Kong martial arts film formula will absolutely adore the meticulously crafted fight scenes. It's easy to overlook or under appreciate the technical aspects of the sets, effects, and minute details related to how the story weaves in and out of the mundane, practical world that we live in and into neighboring realities where things are a bit more... weird. If you can suspend disbelief for a few moments you will find that this film opens up a new perspective on what it means to be who you are to the fullest, whatever that means.

Everything Everywhere All At Once perfectly manages to tell a multiverse story, juggling MANY different genres, from sci-fi, martial arts, black comedy, action and family drama without losing their tone or direction. It somehow manages to tell a realistic and relatable story about family without becoming bogged down by world building when creating its version of the multiverse. 
Speaking of the Quan family, the film does a wonderful job giving an accurate and all-too-relatable representation of Asian family life in North America. The way Evelyn constantly nags Joy about being "too fat", having tattoos, being rebellious and having a white partner is relatable for any Asian kid growing up in North America. All of Evelyn's disappointments in Joy eventually led to her becoming depressed, hence creating the bagel. Hollywood has a long track record of Asian misrepresentation, so to see the struggles of an Asian American family being accurately portrayed on screen is so refreshing to me.  
Along with the realistic and relatable Asian representation, there are some heavy themes revolving around depression, existentialism and nihilism. Just look at how the Everything Bagel is treated; it is a multiversal black hole because Joy pretty much had a psychotic break in one universe and came to believe that nothing truly matters in life. I personally saw this as an allegory for depression as everything about Joy's personality was placed on this Bagel and could never find the good in it, eventually leading to her to enter the black hole as a way to find peace and stop agonizing over a meaningless life. 
These are without a doubt some of the best performances of 2022 so far. Michelle Yeoh was extremely convincing as a woman who's basically always in crisis mode, dealing with her family and business trying to get through an audit. But the true star of the show, is Ke Huy Quan, which is apparently his first movie role in almost 20 years. He is a simple man who is quite happy with his life and is very personable, choosing kindness in the face of negativity and puts everyone else before himself.
Everything Everywhere All at Once is one of the most original films of 2022, delving into family dynamics, mental health, existence, and presenting realistic Asian representation for mainstream audiences. An epic and very personal story with excellent acting, gorgeous cinematography and inventive editing created a movie going experience I have never had before. This is a movie that will not be forgotten by the film community for a very long time.
