The last time I saw a truly creative piece of work from duo filmmakers was a little niche movie that came out in 2016 titled "Swiss Army Man." It is a movie about a depressed man played by The Batman's Paul Dano stranded on a deserted island, on the verge of death until he encounters a corpse that can talk, fart, and be the perfect multi-purpose tool guy played by the one and only, Daniel Radcliffe. It was a weird movie that didn't get much love because of how weird it was. I was one of the few people that legit adored it. My friends even called me weird for liking it. That is until "Everything Everywhere All AT Once" comes out and it basically helps solidify why both this AND "Swiss Army Man."

When the multiverse is at stake, you don't need a magic doctor to save the day. You just need a normal everyday asian woman learning to exploit her true potential as well as encountering some really bizarre dangers that could destroy both her family and the world. Did that make any sense? I hope so because this is a movie that is just TOO hard to describe. It's the kind of movie one needs to experience in theaters. Michelle Yeoh is phenomenal, but the absolute standout is the grown-up version Short Round from "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom" Ke Huy Quan. The man was genuinely fun to watch from start to finish and easily stole the show from me. Jamie Lee Curtis was also a lot of fun to watch. The multiverse stuff is also quite fun and the most unique I've seen compared to both Marvel AND DC. 

My only issue was that the film didn't explain the multiverse concept all that well or perhaps I need to see the movie again as I only saw it once in theaters, so I do hope to get this in 4K at some point. This is one of those movies where you NEED to see it twice. Movies like this NEED to be given more appreciation. I love those Marvel movies, sure, but it is really refreshing when a set of filmmakers that have such really weird ideas get turned into real movies and have people get entertained by that. 

Movies are all about experience, it is all about imagination and when I hear people say they get turned off by weird movies like this or "Swiss Army Man" I get depressed because these are the same people that will have no problem watching a movie featuring a talking Angry Raccoon and a humanoid Tree that only says the same three words every time and make it sound like he is actually saying an actual sentence with only a select few can actually understand him. Yeah because that is NOT weird at all. Don't discriminate against movies of any kind no matter how you feel about the actors, writers, directors, or how the movies market themselves. They all should be viewed and if you don't like that then that is okay as well.The idea of acceptance is really hard to come by and it is weirdly one of the core themes that is presented in this movie. Like I said, I can't explain what even happens in this bizarre fever dream of a movie. You just need to see it for yourself.
Unnecessarily confusing and disjointed. I really cant understand all the extremely high reviews.

Directed with infantile glee by Dan Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (like little boys igniting their farts and burning ants with a magnifying glass), "Everything Everywhere All At Once" is the same old played-out story about evil threatening to destroy the world, repackaged for the short-attention-span generation. Once again, we're in a multiverse, that tired excuse for laziness disguised as imagination. And since nothing needs to make sense in the multiverse, every idea, no matter how idiotic gets lobbed at the wall like monkey-thrown poo, and instantly crammed into the already overloaded script.

And the poor actors. To say the best performance in the film is given by a rock (not Dwayne Johnson, an actual rock) is perhaps unkind but it's unfortunately true. Though they try as hard as humanly possible (and Michelle Yeoh, Stephanie Hsu and Jamie Lee Curtis all get an A-plus for effort), due to the arbitrary nature of the ‘story,' in which disconnected moments are shot willy nilly at the audience with the randomness of a bingo caller, none of the performances are allowed to build: There are no scenes to help the actors create a character; it's all montage.

And after being yanked and shoved from universe to universe at a nauseatingly accelerated pace, never feeling anything but a combination of disorientation and the emotional shutdown that comes from being constantly yelled at, I couldn't tell you how (or if) any of the characters had modulated, or grown or changed. For all I know, Michelle Yeoh may have given the performance of her career. But like the movie itself, the portrayal has no shape: Moments may be occasionally involving but they're not placed in any meaningful sequence, so it doesn't build. And no matter how hard the directors reach for meaning, there is none to be found. The film is a ‘nothing' bagel smeared with every imaginable ingredient but tasting like ashes.

To be fair, the dialog was more often than not swamped by ambient noise in the ridiculously inefficient sound mix, so it's possible that buried under the wet cement score and endless screaming, some hidden significance was revealed. But with all the characters eating snot, mutilating themselves, projectile vomiting, and homophobically shoving things in their butts (just so the audience can go "Ewww! Look, how gross! That guy put something in his butt!"), it's not surprising I may have missed the point.

Even so, there are a few beautiful scenes: In one of the universes, Yeoh is an opera singer, and every time the movie lands on her serenely still, gorgeously lit and costumed character, standing onstage singing (or preparing to sing), the film suddenly works. Mostly because Lux's hectoring, pleading and pummeling score finally calms the fuck down and morphs into something delicate and lovely. But it lasts for all of thirty seconds and then we're off to the demolition derby again, and I'm reaching for the Tylenol.

Then, miraculously, at about the two hour point, after being body-slammed into a stupor, the hyperactive migraine of a movie comes to a sudden stop and we find ourselves on a barren (AND SILENT) mountaintop with two gentle-looking rocks overlooking a prehistoric horizon-wide vista. And, not unlike the feeling you get when your neighbors gardener finally shuts off the leaf blower, or the Novocaine kicks in, or you take your hand out of a pot of boiling water - the relief is so overwhelming that tears are likely to well up your eyes (they did in mine). For a moment, it almost seems as if something profound is about to happen: that all the rubbish leading up to the entrance of the rocks has just been a pretext for showing us what stillness could do, could be. Here, suddenly is the answer to the chronic ‘disorder' threatening the movie's multiverse. Then the directors, (those scamps), afraid that their audience might get bored or reach for their phones, have the rocks start talking to each other via some cutesy subtitles (which is the closest this septically unfunny movie came to making me smile), and we're off, rampaging again.

The final twenty minutes are a repetitious, ungainly grab for validity as Yeoh's mother tries to connect with her unhappy daughter (Hsu) while simultaneously attempting to - wait for it! - stop the multiverse from being sucked into a whirling vortex of nothingness. Yet for all the movie's lip service to the dangers of entropy and depression, "Everything Everywhere All At Once" is actually an open-armed invitation to wallow in both. (The entire experience is so depressing I wouldn't be surprised if Zoloft was a major investor). And contrary to its purported message of hope, it is instead a love letter to chaos. With grim determination (and forced jollity) it backs us into an untenable corner where accepting futility and ‘settling' seem to be the only solution. Where (to use Orwellian doublespeak) "Conforming IS Rebellion."

Everything Everywhere All at Once (A+)
To say this movie is a brilliant blend of so many different genres and entirely fresh would be putting it mildly. This film doesn't fit squarely into any one genre with some of the funniest comedy, craziest action, emotionally family moments, and craziest outright insanity I have ever seen in an film. It is truly a film which deserves more recognition and proves the common phrase that "films are no longer original" completely wrong.

This movie which follows Evelyn (wonderfully played by Michelle Yeoh), a middle aged Asian American who is just trying to stay afloat but is suddenly met with some life altering interventions from alternate universe that exist in different timelines. Think the Spiderman movie that just came out but a more grounded and actually well thought out approach. Evelyn is taught how to travel back and forth through these realities and gain the skills of her alternate selves in unorthodox ways. I don't want to spoil anymore of the plot but just based off that small premise I stated above you could see how this film could capitalize on so many different ideas and unique takes on alternate timelines.

This movie goes insane about 20 minutes in and doesn't let off that insanity one but throughout the film. Sometimes movies have ambitious ideas like this film but fail to compile it all together in a way that makes any sense or is intriguing. This film does the almost impossible with having such ambitious goals but delivering this ambition in a way that is highly palatable and actually moving.

The runtime being long in this film is a great thing because there is so many different ideas  and themes that are explored and limiting the time would be to not fully explore these ideas/themes. There was a couple moments in this film where you think that it is over but nope you just witnessed a mere portion of what this film was aiming to offer. In the latter half with every extra scene I was feeling my emotions getting stronger and stronger towards these characters. You get to take a hugely introspective look at each individual character and why they are the way they are. I loved slowly peeling back the layers to each character you see on screen and understanding what motivates them not only in the original timeline you start in but also the multiverse timelines as well. The way we learn about the characters through multiple realities is really unique and done expertly. I felt a genuine sadness, happiness and frustration when looking at the characters through all these lenses.

The way the film is shot, the whole premise of the film, the direction, and the choreography of action scenes was all meticulously out together in what I can only imagine to be hours on hours of brilliant minds collaborating. On top of this the acting was superb across the board. The lead played by Michelle Yeoh drives the movie forward as she acts as a vehicle to put all the movies themes on to. Ke Hey Quan does a brilliant job as the lighthearted husband of the lead and acts as a through line of heart and integrity throughout. Then their daughter who is played by Stephanie Hsu is expertly played as a distancing family member who is going through a lot of early adulthood emotions. Many different heavy topics like divorce and homosexuality are brought to attention in this film and I have no doubt that the smooth way they were able to tackle these heavy topics was because of this cast that does such a believable job. Also Jamie Lee Curtis has a side character that recurs which steals the show anytime it is on screen.

I must warn those reading this review and seeing the praise from others that this film can be hard to get into at first and also very difficult to wrap your head around entirely. I plead that you try to understand the vision that the filmmakers had for this and fully immerse yourself in this vision. If you do that I feel you can have an experience like I had where you become fully locked in and taken back by the over all film. One small gripe towards the film is that there is a couple comedic scenes that felt a little uncomfortable to watch and not fully my sense of humor but I could totally see liking those scenes and my distaste for them is not because they were not made or thought out properly but rather just didn't mesh with my personal taste. 

So overall go watch this film that was made by A24. It is a good time and is sure to keep you entertained and engaged. If you love artsy films and movies that really show that passion went into the craft than you are sure to find something here to love.

Some folks view the ending "return to family and love" as cliche and find the scene in stone universe to be much more touching, yet I was personally most impressed by this cliche ending. Here is why.

I went to watch the film without any spoiler - only knowing it was about multi universe. 
First thought it was only a good construction of interesting  sci-fi settings.
Then gathered it aims to discuss about self-identity of first and second generation immigrants, East-Asia family relationship and contemporary society topics.
After 1 hour sitting there, I believed I was hearing the howling of Existentialism.
At the last quarter of film, I finally realized to my surprise that this might actually be a story about Chan (Zen).

In section 10 of <Diamond Sutra>, there is such text
"Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thusly give rise to a clear and pure mind — a mind not associated with abiding in form; a mind not associated with abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, sensations, or dharmas; a mind not abiding in life."

The first half shows that everything is meaningless - form, sounds, scents, tastes, sensations, your perception, your goals, your ambitions, your expectations on yourself and others around you - everything does not have a constant, perpetual, self-sufficient meaning, this fact is shown and it is beyond argument.
But this is not the end of story, it follows:
Above all the meaninglessness, there must arise a clear and pure mind, a mind not abiding to any particular meaning.
Where does this word "must" come from? Meaninglessness is not a state that mind could abide to, therefore mind must arise in itself and perceive meanings as is.
It follows naturally that the second half of film would illustrate how such a clear and pure mind arises and perceives "love and family" as is.

While "seeing meaninglessness" is nontrivial, it is still possible for human beings living in modern society to approach this state with the everlasting flow of social ideological trend and fluctuations in personalities. On the other hand, "giving rise to a clear and pure mind", "facing the life in a calm and non-contentious way" is far more delicate.

I'll attempt to give a translation of film title in Chan (Zen) concepts:
《一切时中诸世界所有法》
All at Once • 一切时中 • 过去心不可得 现在心不可得 未来心不可
Everywhere • 诸世界 • 如來说世界 即非世界 是名世界
Everything • 所有法 • 一切法皆是佛法 • 所言一切法者 即非一切法 是故名一切法 • 我说法 如筏喻者 法尚应舍 何况非法

After 2016's Daniel Radcliff farting corpse film introduced us to the quirky inventive madness of Dan Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, a pair of co-writers/directors known collectively as Daniels, they have upped their game with their follow-up, a multiverse film that's as good as, if not better than, what Marvel can muster, but on a fraction of their budget. The always fantastic Michelle Yeoh and Ke Huy Quan are the Wangs who run a family laundromat being audited by Jamie Lee Curtis's IRS agent. Throw in Stephanie Hsu's lesbian daughter and James Hong's traditional Gong Gong and what we have is a well-observed Asian-American intergenerational family drama dressed up with science-fiction bells and whistles and what's technically classified as fairly lo-fi special effects, though they're no less effective for it. With the rules of the multiverse and increasingly ridiculous instructions for jumping between them subversively dispensed with in the duration of an elevator ride, their screenplay manages to just about contain itself within its own logic and make it makes sense, and with that exposition out of the way, the rest is a fast-paced kinetic joyride (with an exhausted editor afterwards) through alternate universes where a brilliant and gamed cast are given ample opportunities to play distinctively different characters while the Daniels lobe everything from cinematic riffs on Ratatouille, 2001, and naturally HK cinema as represented by the extremities that are Jackie Chan action comedy and Wong Kai Wai's melancholic romanticism to random surrealism like hotdog fingers and subtitled rocks onto the screen. If admittedly it drags a little towards the end as it piles on very conventional and sentimental cliches to concoct its crowd-pleasing love-is-the-answer ending, it remains bizarrely entertaining, visually arresting and narratively chaotic and bonkers all at once, and I can't wait to see it again.

Our thoughts, feelings, and opinions don't make sense to our parents in some ways as the rapid changing and development both in China and America, but they are always there no matter what and support us for no reason. They always try their best to give us the best. "It doesn't make sense but I am there."
I was also touched by another thing that the director wanna deliver, "What if". What if Wang didn't abandon all they had in Hong Kong and come to the US from the very beginning. Maybe she won't need to accept that her daughter is dating another girl and deal with the shit like tax report. 
Illusion is always perfect since it isn't real.

This film is astounding.

Daniels have managed to give the concept of the multiverse (a trope already starting to overextend itself) new life and new purpose on film, which is no small feat. Wrapped up in this insanely frenetic and propulsive film is a story that centers on family, catharsis, love, kindness, violence, nihilism, acceptance, friendship, hope, loss, and… buttplugs.

Reading that last sentence, you might get the wrong impression that this movie feels somewhat unfocused or too widespread to connect all of those dots. But like the movie's multiverse, they all stem from one single point in the narrative, and that focus aids in creating a story that flits easily between each emotional beat Daniels have lined up for the audience.

The main character of Evelyn Wang is the central focus of the story, and Michelle Yeoh is the absolute perfect actor to play her. This is undoubtedly her best work in years, not only showcasing her still incredible prowess as an on-screen fighter, but the depth of her ability to bring characters to life—sometimes with laser-focused nuance, sometimes with wild hilarity, and sometimes with unabashed heart. She breathes the air of this film and it's story so easily.

And the rest of the cast—Stephanie Hsu as Joy, Ke Huy Quan as Waymond, James Hong as Gong, and Jaimie Lee Curtis as Dierdre—are so perfectly cast it's impossible to watch this film and not be bowled over by the sheer talent they have. Ke Huy Quan and Stephanie Hsu are particularly effecting in their roles as Evelyn's husband and daughter, respectively, and they have moments in the third act so full of genuine honesty and emotion that it brought me to tears.

Also notable is the unbelievably good stunt choreography, the special effects, and the editing. The fight scenes are married with brilliant practical effects and CGI (done by just FIVE people!) and together, they call back to the best of Hong Kong and American action cinema—from Jackie Chan's entire career of frantic-seeming choreography, to Yeoh's own masterful display in ‘Crouching Tiger', to Keanu Reeves in ‘The Matrix', and many, many others. It's a love letter to movement and action, and it feels so good to watch unfold. All of this is held together with some of the best editing I've ever seen in a film. With pacing that ratchets back and forth between methodical to otherworldly, Paul Rogers' has done a perfect job marrying each of the emotional story beats and action set pieces into a cohesive and eminently watchable work of art.

Lastly, the film looks amazing. It's lush and beautiful, with shifting colors and textures mixed into a kaleidoscopic experience. Larkin Seiple deserves every accolade for making multiple universes feel grounded and somehow real.

Despite the hype, I do not believe this movie is about an unlikely savior of the universe of universes. Rather, it is an exploration of one woman's struggle to maintain loving relationships with her daughter, husband, and father in the face of life's relentless drive towards chaos and mediocrity. I saw the multiverse sideshow as reflective of her own regrets at the choices not taken, how she wished to impose her desires on those of her family, and how little she actually knew about theirs.

The extended metaphor goes on much too long, with a few totally unnecessary sidetracks. For example, a good ten minutes is devoted to the man with a raccoon on his head. All of this could have been left out, and the film still would have kept its narrative arc and made its points. The Daniels had a lot of fun riffing on kung-fu movies, film noir, and a raft of science fiction from the past (Matrix, anyone?) But a few hot-dog fingers and slow-motion butt jokes go a long way, and could have been trimmed a bit

With more discipline and a sharper eye towards what they were trying to do, these guys could have had the next Groundhog Day or Ghostbusters. Instead, we're left with an overlong but pleasant evening's entertainment for the intellectually savvy.

Here's how this movie talked to me, personally.

The movie couldn't have come out at a better time. The last few years have been tough for all of us. It feels as though we've been served all the bad everything everywhere all at once. Not a single stone has been left unturned. After the last few years of a long, wild and scary rollercoaster of worldwide struggles, this movie comes out to remind us that nothing matters, but not in the extreme nihilistic way you'd probably expect.

It teaches us that there's beauty in nihilism to be found. We just need to make an effort to search for it. It reminds us that our little struggles or big world problems don't matter. 

They say that your life flashes before your eyes upon your death, reminding you of everything everywhere all at once - your life, the joys of life and the struggles of life, things you may have long forgotten, decisions you made, both good and bad, and past experiences, both positive and negative. Some may experience regret but most certainly hope to experience happiness and feel a sense of fulfilment at the end of their journey, as they get closure to the light at the end of the tunnel (bagel). 

If this is all true, then, to me, this magical movie is the embodiment of that experience, with a little twist. It pulls us out of the void of the bagel. It pulls us away from the light at the end of the tunnel back into our bodies, creating a much stronger sense of self and giving us a second chance at our life. It teaches us that at the end of the day, it's the people closest to us, our family and friends, and our relationships with them are the only thing that matters. It gives us a second chance and an opportunity to experience and flash through our lives, everything everywhere all at once, and go back and make peace with ourselves, who we are, and amend relationships with the people that matter the most, our family and friends, and start truly and genuinely appreciate what we have so that when the time comes, there's no space for regret, but joy! There is not a single negative thing about this movie and this whole experience, not even one thing to nitpick.

Now, I think that some people may take points away for the length of the movie, but for me personally, length is rarely an issue, especially if the people behind the movie have evidently this much genuine passion, love and respect for the arts of movie making and have put this much blood, sweat and effort into it. Extremely talented, resourceful and creative artists, visionaries and risk-takers such as "The" Daniels and their crew of world-class actors such as "The" Michelle Yeoh, "The" Stephanie Hsu, "The" Ke Huy Quan and "The" Jamie Lee Curtis and "The" wonderful stunt people, SFX and practical effects crew must be celebrated. Finally! A multiverse movie with imagination, soul, and delightful absurdity! This is art in its highest form. Beneath its dazzling surface, this movie teases out deep questions about modern life.

Until recently, all of human history was a struggle for survival. Today, our lives are so comfortable that we are faced with a completely different kind of problem: too many choices.

Is our multitude of choices a blessing, or a curse?

Life in a hunter-gatherer society was nasty, brutish, and short. Our path in life was mostly predetermined: just try to survive and reproduce. But the few good moments could be fully savored and enjoyed, because that's all there was.

We evolved to survive as hunter-gatherers, so we are maladapted for modern society. With all of our survival needs met, our biggest challenge is to wrestle with our own vestigial cognitive biases. 

With so many life paths available to us, our cognitive bias focuses on the drawbacks of the choices we make, while conversely focusing on the benefits of the choices we didn't make.

Should I have chosen the other University? Did I choose the right course of study? Is this really my most self-actualizing career path? Should I have married the other person I dated? Do I want to have children, and if so how many?

The presence of these choices is an indicator of a pretty good life.

But if we get stuck doting on choices not taken, it's harder to appreciate the positive aspects of the life we chose. In this way, having many choices is a burden, because when the path we chose turns out to be imperfect, we blame ourselves for not having chosen differently.

In reality–in every possible reality, there are always imperfections. If we can learn to accept that every choice, even the best choice, has drawbacks, then we can free ourselves to more deeply appreciate the benefits of the path we find ourselves on presently.

The concept of multiverse here is the same used in the MCU, but while at Marvel the concept is still theoretical, here we can see it in practice. There are at least six parallel stories that never run over each other and are extremely well developed (if this movie doesn't win Best Original Screenplay at the Academy Awards there's no justice in the world). I have a lot to say about the cast but this is a movie that doesn't allow spoilers. It's normal to feel that the third act is a little dragged, I felt it too, but as in "Uncut Gems", it's an understandable decision, because the rhythm is in line with what the character is feeling and the situation she is going through. I would say something about the ending but even the minor comparison can be a spoiler. In a nutshell, watch this film as soon as you can!

While the movie might take a lot of time and go through a lot of complex and confusing scenes, they all add up to a wholesome ending that's sure to make anyone appreciate the movie. In my opinion the best thing this movie does is find a way to explore the dynamic of family relations, and it's portrayal is more than realistic, the directors are grounded in this regard, from the precarious and   love- hate relationship Evelyn and Joy have, to the problem filled marriage between Waymond and Evelyn, surprisingly enough it even shows the anxiety Joy has in navigating loving a girl and coming out to her grandfather; that is one of the best things about this movie. The next thing I think it explores really well is the idea of free choice, (not to be pretentious but) it does make the Kierkegaardian point that anxiety is the dizziness of choice, by showing the protagonist, Evelyn, explore all the choices she ever made in her life, and how by making different choices her life led to completely different paths most of them being more successful than the life path she currently was in, and how this affects her psychologically. We then get to see the difference between her reaction to that and her daughters' reaction to finding this out, landing her daughter to arrive at the classic cosmic nihilist point "That nothing in the world matters," while this has been explored in so many classic movies and Tv Series so may times, the feel of this movie is different because for some time the characters do agree with this, until the climax of the movie happens and takes a turn in the direction of Existential Nihilism, and tries to save all the characters. This movie, at first almost seemed like Rick and Morty (which I am a fan of) but unlike it the family dynamic is more realistic, I digress. While the philosophical idea of the movie and ideas brought up are handled well, the next thing I would like to address is the sheer cinematic and directing style of the movie, the choreography, acting and emotions expressed are truly magnificent and aid towards the story telling. This is an instant classic movie in my opinion, it's not too heavy and not too light, honestly my best movie of the year. The sound design had me on my toes, the editing tore me from my own reality into many others, and the heart-tugging themes across the beautiful chaos were nothing short of breathtaking to experience. It is both hilarious and dramatic, with a handful of questionable juvenile moments that are purely subjective to your taste, but in its entirety, is still weird and wonderful. This is what movie magic looks, sounds and feels like.

There are some bold and over the top choices made in this movie that won't land with everyone, but they sure as hell landed with me. Everything Everywhere All At Once
In just about every sense, this movie delivered what the title promised. It's so easy to get sucked into with all there is to appreciate about it. Michelle Yeoh leads the cast in her portrayal of Evelyn Quan and her multiverse counterparts. The version of her we focus on is a middle-aged mother who immigrated to the United States from China with her husband, Waymond Wang. They own a laundromat, raise a daughter, struggle to pay bills and spend their days daydreaming of all the things that could have been, while trying to find some level of joy in each other. Evelyn has revelations about herself and her motherhood, largely to her daughter Joy, played by Stephanie Hsu - a now-adult who is very different but also, in so many ways, an image of her. Hsu does a good job at playing all the different versions of herself, with emotional vulnerability, depth, and emotional range. The character felt very raw, real, and there was lot to explore about her.
The editing did a brilliant job in illustrating an incredibly believable multi-dimensional world all colliding into these characters' love for each other extending across space and time. As the aspect ratio shifts, the tone switches; in 16:9, it breaks itself from the world and switches into a more comic-book feel. The characters are almost in a cartoon and this makes this medium and theme an engaging way to tell the story. Not a whole lot of CGI editing was used in this movie but they still did a really good job at accomplishing a fantastical world and all its different possibilities and timelines. The repetition of the front desk marks the beginning of each chapter while representing a story that goes backwards and forwards in time and space, yet is experienced by one character sequentially. The emotional depth makes everyone watching feel seen in their raw humanity.

Easily one of the most visually striking and conceptually original films of the 21st century, Everything Everywhere All At Once may have a cumbersome title, and an occasionally confusing to the point of tedium storyline, but its chock full of incredible ingenuity and genuine emotional weight. Michelle Yeoh, who in the last few years is finally getting the recognition she deserves, plays a downtrodden laundromat owner who is introduced to the secrets of the multiverse. The film has a similar problem to Inception and Tenet, in that the story is so complicated that lengthy scenes of exposition are required, and even those can make it feel more difficult to comprehend. But as the story progress you do develop something of a handle on things, and when you grasp the core concepts the film really comes into its own. I loved the way it handled themes of nihilism, family acceptance and the importance of understanding a person despite their differences, and while the middle section of the film can feel long and directionless at times, as it enters the 3rd act the film delivers some serious emotional gut punches, and everything that we've seen falls into place. The actors do a great job, the script is funny, insightful and cleverly constructed, and the lessons we learn come about completely organically. It's a film that many will find hard to digest, but if the cinematic medium is going to continue to evolve, we need films that are going to push boundaries and break new ground, and that's what this one does. If you can embrace its wackiness and accept its unconventionality, then you're in for a real treat.

‘The Matrix in The Multiverse of Madness', that's a description that feels both fitting and yet entirely undersells this multi-faceted feast for the senses, and boy, is it absurdly good. The result is something with a bit of everything: creative visuals, action and humour, but also has a powerful human core whose heartfelt, deeper messages effectively penetrate all the madness. The cast do a superb job – both Stephanie Hsu and Jamie Lee Curtis are great, and it's really nice to see Ke Huy Quan on the silver screen again -- but this is Michelle Yeoh's show and she gets her chance to shine like a crazy diamond. This is a unique, wild, fun and touching ride, and there's about a million ways this couldn't and probably shouldn't have worked, but Daniels have outdone themselves to deliver something truly spectacular. One of the most enjoyable films I've seen in recent memory.

Tour De Force.  As if the Matrix could be re-incarnated, now half breed, holding both the memories of Neo and that of Charles Frost.  The digitally aware self meets the self reminiscent, combine that with the duality of the chaos and order of life, and you have a brilliant film.  Humor intertwines this epic tale of life; equal parts tormentor, and angelic savior, the main character bouts with not only their internal narrative, but also that which seems to order and disorder the universe.  Intermixed with this narrative is a parents look at their own dreams through the life of their daughter, who becomes their own duality.  Projecting the dreams of one onto the decisions of another.  Once again chaos intervenes.  This repeats itself until the creator relents, the protagonists find peace, and two rocks find moments to simply be in the existence.  This would be a fine place to be, if not for the chaos of life drawing one to be more than just a rock, but to be both active and aware, not only presently but infinitely.  And that is the conundrum of what it means to be human.  To be Everything, Everywhere, All At Once.  Aware of who you are now, what it took to bring you to today, all of the possibilities that could have made up to tomorrow, and you here we are now, experiencing it, all at once.  This movie could define a generation and yet define everyone.  Like Citizen Kane, or The Matrix, Everything, Everywhere, All at Once provides a glimpse at what it means to exist with more knowledge than ever, of what our existence could have been, meanwhile in our actual existence, we are in ever more demand, if only we were present to feel and absorb what that should mean to, both the ying and the yang.  The order and the chaos, the joy and the pain.  The duality of mans existence.  Rarely does a movie summarize such valuable truths, and ever rare is it that said truths are displayed in a captivating and visually entertaining narrative.  I fear only that we won't really understand what it means, but then again, why should anyone be so silly as to assume they do.

Reminds of or watch alongside:

- The Princess Bride - Similar family fun, with some fantastic action, and a heartwarming story that keeps you rooting for its characters' adventures!

- The Matrix - Chose this due to its use of the multiverse/anything can happen rhetoric and acquiring skills from the experiences shared/learnt via a headset. Oh, and it definitely throws some punches!

"In my opinion...":

A24 did not disappoint with this release. Starting slow to help you learn the roles of the characters. 

As I am not an Asian living in the US, I still found this film to be engaging and allow audience members to share the experiences of each character through the medium of the multiverse segments. 

Also includes scenes that relate to the dynamics of every family's peaks and troths: love, becoming misunderstood/estranged, and the battle to uphold their roles in the relationships that are shared between them. 

And then. 'Everything...' moulds itself into the fun and ridiculous. I was captivated and felt connected to the multiple story arcs that are presented to us. Always returning to its 'That is just silly' method.

This film will make you laugh and cry. I was utterly captivated. 

Although, it does have A LOT to say. I can understand why some viewers may be put off by the ever-changing pace, a complex sci-fi environment and it does help to have some awareness of Asian culture within the US to fully grasp its messages.

Other than that:

Come for the hotdogs, stay for the punches.

The film title for "Everything Everywhere All at Once" is its best possible plot summary.  The film is chaotic, disorienting, innovative, thought-provoking, undisciplined and profoundly moving.  It's impossible to summarize briefly.  But "Everything …" is also the best reason to venture out to a movie theater since the pandemic began over two years ago.

Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert – the Daniels - who co-wrote and co-directed this film, are veterans of several movie shorts and music videos.  Their previous feature film, 2016's "Swiss Army Man," is summarized by IMDb as follows:  "A hopeless man stranded on a desert island befriends a dead body, and together they go on a surreal journey to get home."  In "Everything …" they graduate from mundane topics like human mortality to tackle the multiverse.

The idea of the multiverse posits that there are an infinite number of universes – "alternate universes" or "parallel universes" – where the consequences of all the choices we make or don't make are played out to their logical conclusions.  It's an idea that has been endorsed by Stephen Hawking and Neil deGrasse Tyson.  But philosophically, it's a pretty depressing brand of nihilism: how can life have meaning if none of our choices really matter?

The Daniels use the multiverse for two purposes.  First, when characters jump from one alternate universe to another, the moviegoer can explore the alternate life stories of the primary characters, particularly Evelyn (a spectacular Michelle Yeoh - 2000's "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon") who is an unhappily married, dissatisfied co-owner of a laundromat whose main achievement has been disappointing her father.  But in alternate universes where she has made different choices, Evelyn is, variously, a famous singer, a star of martial arts films, a sign-twirler on the street, a resident of a universe where everyone has hotdogs instead of fingers and, most poignantly, one of two sentient rocks on an uninhabitable planet (the most touching scenes in the film).  Evelyn bounces from one universe to another to help her struggling daughter Joy (yes, I do see the irony) who, as many parents would predict, is both a confused young adult and also Jobu Tupaki, an arch-villain bent on destroying the multiverse.  In one scene, Joy/Jobu confides that she has used her superpowers to place all the important things in the world in a bagel (you got it:  an "everything bagel").

The Daniels also use alternate universes to explore core concepts around family dynamics: the paralytic effect of parental disapproval; the notion that a family member's quiet inaction sometimes represents kindness and strength, not passivity; and finally the strong suggestion that parental love is the most powerful force in the universe.
  
At the end of the day, this weirdly wonderful film shares a powerful theme with the Bible, the Torah, the Koran and almost any good Kurt Vonnegut novel: in a confusing, scary, sometimes brutal universe, we'd all be better off if we all treated one another with a little more kindness.

Yeoh, Man! -  Film Review: Everything Everywhere All At Once ★★★★1/2

Have you ever felt that the films of Baz Luhrmann and Michael Bay dragged a little? Do you need more edits? Faster action? More kablooey and kablam? Well, to paraphrase SNL's Stefan, "America's hottest movie, Everything Everywhere All At Once has everything! Talking  Rocks! Hot dog fingers! Backwards whooshing office chairs! A Sharpie wielding Halloween star!" Who knew, however, that it would live up to that hype and more, easily becoming one of the best films of 2022? 

The Daniels, Dan Kwan and Daniel Schienert, who last brought us the delightfully fantastical Swiss Army Man, return with an explosive (although with no farts this time) yet beautifully character-driven film which is literally about, as the title implies, EVERYTHING. Michelle Yeoh plays Evelyn Wang, a downtrodden laundromat owner who lives a financially desperate, hard-working life with her husband Waymond (the triumphant return of Ke Huy Kwan best known for his roles in Indiana Jones And The Temple Of Doom and Goonies), daughter Joy (Stephanie Hsu of The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel) and Grandpa Gong Gong (James Hong). 

When we meet Evelyn, she's exhausted from her work load, strained in her marriage, and dreading an upcoming meeting with the IRS. Enter Jamie Lee Curtis, in an unforgettable performance, as Deirdre Beaubeirdra, a joyless tax auditor who has never met a part of her body she hasn't scratched. She has it out for the Wangs, issuing an ultimatum to get their receipts together or face the consequences. With all of the pressure reaching a boiling point and seemingly no way out, a surprise twist throws Evelyn and her family into one insane adventure after another, fracturing timelines, universes, and offering up a "Sliding Doors on Acid" premise guaranteed to make the most kinetic of directors green with envy. It gets very complicated with its kitchen sink approach, with some interludes feeling random or interchangeable, but I found it worth the ticket price alone for the image of Curtis flying in slow motion through the air to face off against Yeoh in just one of many heartstopping moments. Special mention must go to Larkin Seiple for his phenomenal cinematography, Shirley Kurata for ten films worth of insightful, memorable costume design, and Jason Kisvarday's production design, which features an impressive, memorable array of styles. 

Through it all, Yeoh navigates the impossible, playing a huge swath of characters, explosively executing complicated action sequences, and making us feel something deeply for our central heroine. She's giving the performance of her career here, able to capture our hearts while concurrently displaying the entire gamut of brittle neuroses in her wheelhouse. She plays so many different characters, some seemingly autobiographical, all of whom have a level of confidence and empowerment lacking in Evelyn herself. 

When Waymond steps in to motivate her, the movie really takes off with a series of brilliantly executed action sequences. Kwan, whose voice seems to have not aged a day, keeps up with Yeoh, delivering a heartfelt, fun, fast and furious performance all while doing flips and kicks guaranteed to earn him Instant Hunk status. It's so wonderful to have him back after years of giving up on acting. Here's to many more films to come. 

Also of note is Hsu, who starts off as the detached daughter who her family for not fully supporting her queerness. She, like the rest of her relatives, finds her own special superpowers, elevating her to icon status before the film ends. Who wouldn't want this badass to kick down a few doors for them? I was also very touched by the mother-daughter relationship depicted here. It succinctly gives so many young queer people the tools and language for having tough conversations with their parents. Kudos to this slam bang film for having educational purpose too, filled as it is with nuance and grace far beyond what one expects from a genre film.

Movie's biggest fail: Grotesque normalization of family abuse. 
Warning: animal abuse presented as humor.  (Played for laughs) where the small dog on a leash is swung across the room, first being thrown into a refrigerator, then again being swung around by the neck and thrown across the room, slamming into a wall divider and crying. 
The worst part of this though, was it was clearly written by two men who have zero understanding of the severe consequences of mother-to-daughter emotional battery.  Script seems to have been written to appeal to the same Boomers who said millenials were lazy and poor because 'they ate too much avocado toast'.  Skip forward a decade, replace 'avocado toast' with 'everything bagel' and now it's Gen Z who are selfish, lazy, self-centered, cruel, while 'poor hardworking ma' tried so hard despite her vicious, ungrateful loser of a kid bla bla bla.  

Notably, the mom never apologizes or makes any kind of amends for the damage she did and continues to do to her daughter, but apparently imagines her daughter as a sad, tacky, angry dump in attention-grabbing outfits, and the mom openly resents giving birth to her. 
The scene where she comes at her daughter with a box-cutter razor, also punches her daughter in the face, and the daughter lies and tells her dad she fell on the sofa was the end for me.  I kept watching, hoping this was the run-up to some drastic turnaround and self-realization at the end... but no.  
Both the mom character and the writers seem to have no clue as to why abuse victims leave their abusers. Being male writers, they understood why the abused *husband* filed for divorce papers, but couldn't quite grasp why the abused daughter would also deserve to leave. The rock scene was a great example of how much they failed to 'get it'. Could have been poignant if it weren't for the fact the mom couldn't do basic, fundamental things to make her daughter feel safe, like supporting her against her abusive grandfather, supporting her choice to date another woman, or at least at the bare minimum, stop calling her fat and destroying her self-esteem.  But we're supposed to believe the mom would jump off a cliff to follow her daughter LOL.  The sappy ending where the daughter shrugs off all of this lifetime of abuse and parental rejection as 'just me being dramatic... awkward' was pathetic and the upsetting downer of the whole film.  Never saw the abused dad figure saying, 'gee, let's call off the divorce and be a happy family again, this divorce stuff was just me being too dramatic'.  No. This if anything underlined the worst part of the film, the stereotypical expectation that women, especially, girls, are supposed to accept abuse and forgive their abusers and 'let it go'.

The normalization of family abuse and animal abuse was absolutely the most grotesque and unforgivable things about this film and I am sorry I spent $5 renting it. What ultimately ends up being so impressive about Everything Everywhere All At Once is how simple its story really is, but how wildly complex of a route it takes to tell it. It's a story about generational trauma, grass is always greener thinking, and self acceptance, but what we see is kung fu, high kingdoms worshipping a bagel, rocks in a desert talking to each other, and Jamie Lee Curtis stapling paper to her forehead. It's incredibly inventive film making that is at times so inventive that it is difficult to keep up with. I, let alone anyone, is wholly unfamiliar with movies like this because they just don't exist. On top of being innovative, EEAAO is funny, smart, and feels like a grand adventure of epic scale with its grandiose visuals and  sweeping musical score. I don't think I could praise an edit of a movie more than this one. That said, it's middle third is tough to for me to remain wholly invested in due to its sheer absurdity. Some people will love that, some will bounce off it a bit. Either way, I really liked this and respect the hell out of it.

"The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" is a modern sci-fi classic. It also inspired a glut of art-school string theorists. Their latest offering is "EEAAO" - a visually overstimulating, philosophically vapid attempt at an existential statement. I had hoped this brand of quirky nihilist humanism would die when Rick and Morty was cancelled. This film is like watching Neil DeGrasse Tyson's "Cosmos" on molly.
While the acting is uniformly excellent, and the action sequences are well directed, the weak screenwriting belies Daniels' apparent confidence in their art. The "grand statement" that subjective experience and emotion gives meaning to an objectively meaningless existence is  questionable, as this worldview has no greater philosophical power than the conventional worldviews that Daniels' spend two and a half hours gleefully undermining. This could've been an excellent family drama that engages maturely with the philosophical questions that Daniels' seem so keenly aware of. I guess they were too busy beating existential morality to death with a dildo to care.

This happens every now and then when a film garners support to such an overwhelming degree that I grow more worried to actually see it. I guess what I'm saying is I don't like having expectations; yet another reason why  I avoid trailers like the bubonic plague. So I, regrettably, walked into this movie filled with expectations. I am happy to report that some were irrefutably fulfilled, and some were not. The unsung heroes of post-production are largely responsible for the former as Paul Rogers delivers a stellar performance in the editing chair. Speaking of stellar performances, it is about time that Michelle Yeoh be recognized for her immense talent. Oscar-winning talent as Evelyn? I'm not so sure. Nonetheless, I thoroughly enjoyed her "baby deer learning how to walk" in the context of a multiverse---pure entertainment. Stephanie Hsu as the ironically named Joy and Ke Huy Quan as Waymond fill in the gaps beautifully and bring the screenplay back down to reality in moments where it is needed most to reveal a touching familial undertone that is crucial for the success of the exposition. My issues arise in pacing. After doing the intense field work of asking two of my friends it is clear that I am not unique in thinking this way. While this is certainly not the first film to deal heavily with a multiverse, introduction to said multiverse is key. As viewer of generation z, it seems concerning how often I had to play catch up. I think this issue in understanding begins at the first sight of the multiverse. There is not enough time for audience digestion of one particular plot point so when it comes time to introduce another (which is extremely quickly with this film), it seems easier to just give up and be confused. I shouldn't have to rely on my own willingness to decode to enjoy the supposed, "most entertaining movie of the year". This said, the innovation and just flat out ridiculousness of Everything Everywhere All At Once far outweighs any conception issues I had with it. You know a movie is keeping you engaged when you stare at two rocks in conversation completely enamored. Is this the greatest movie ever made? I don't think so. Will it make you feel something? Yes. Definitely not one to miss out on.

The plot itself is extremely simple (not sure why a few have issues with understanding it).  If you don't want to follow the crazy universe hopping, which I can understand for older folk, it can be broken down to it's most simple of parts into a story about a fractured family with one single character in the very middle and mostly the cause of said familial problems.  The main character goes on an absolutely crazy adventure through different universes where they experience their life in completely different ways from the one they currently lead and the story plays out showing the effect of knowing such information has on them.
Heartfelt moments throughout the movie just made everything come together so perfectly. 

This movie deserves awards.

The movie has a  "Multiverse" like element but it doesn't bring it up multiple times. It allows us to absorb that information without it being annoying. This is how a Multiverse movie should be in my honest opinion. 

The movie does start off slow but it's to get a feel of each character and their personalities giving us an insight on how they behave and adapt throughout the film. 

The Action Scenes are Jackie Chan meets Kung Fu Hustle and it's done so well that you welcome these moments within the movie. 

Throughout the movie there are some moments that are uncanny, but to be honest. These moments don't come off very welcoming but they serve a purpose later on in the movie that provides an important role later on in the movie making it very hilarious, it gives you that "Oh now I see why that was placed there." "Oh that's why (Dot Dot Dot)" It doesn't make sense but later on it will add further humor to certain scenes throughout the movie. 

 You'll see exactly what I mean if you do decide on watching it.  

It does have some dark comedy, so this is not something for children. 
16+ should be fine. (Swearing) (Some Blood During Fight Scenes) (Mild uses of certain erotic toys) But (No Nudity) 

This movie was just outstanding overall. I loved the Characters and the Actors felt natural and the emotions were genuine. You can feel for each moment good, bad, awesome, weird, and understand that this is how a movie should be.

It's absolutely hilarious, gut-wrenching, wholesome, and even full of fantastically choreographed fight scenes all in a fantastic blend.  Even in the times when things become sad, they throw in some comedy that doesn't truly feel like it takes away from the moment but it does help alleviate the "feels" a bit. (Especially when the plot hits close to home for a lot of people)  I was able to laugh and cry at the same time without feeling like I was stretched too thin.

While I feel like the message behind the movie is extremely simple and can portrayed even without the crazy shenanigans of universe-hopping, this insanity is what gives the movie the character it needed to really elevate itself into something special.  Hell, the most touching moment in the movie for me was in one of these different universes and even though it was hilarious, I was still touched by the moment despite being able to laugh.

Heck, even though the movie is quite long (for me at least) it never felt like it was overstaying it's welcome and I never had that feeling of "okay, let's wrap this up." that I feel with 90% of movies in the theater.

Heavily recommend to most people, if they can deal with the off-the-wall shenanigans that occur. 
"Everything Everywhere All At Once" is an absolute tour de force on every sense you could experience from a film. In spans of less than five minutes, you could experience laughter, joy, confusion, anger, depression, fear, etc. as the story tells itself. The visuals, camera work, acting, choreography, costumes, lighting, sound design, set designs, EVERYTHING are flawlessly executed. There isn't a single moment where the movie isn't screaming for your attention. Through all that noise, there is a very deep, relatable, and real story of generational trauma, finding yourself, dealing with your flaws, and fighting to be who you are and for your family to understand you for it. Daniels have wowed me before with Swiss Army Man, my favorite movie of 2016. And now this film is my favorite of 2022, and perhaps even if the last five years. Do yourself a favor and give yourself a night to watch through this film, chew on it, and ask yourself if you're living your best life. A beautifully masterful film, a true masterpiece of it's time for sure, and hopefully will inspire other generations in the future.

It told a simple story of the love and miscommunications between an immigrant mother and her gay daughter, as well as a distant wife and sensitive husband (both hardworking), in a crazy complex and confusingly beautiful way. The visuals were just as amazing. I was drawn in the whole time and sobbing through half of it. It was truly an experience and something more screenwriters and directors should look up to. The performances were great. Ke Huy Quan was incredible and one of the highlights of the entire movie. His switch from clueless doppy husband to multi-versal warrior had me hysterically laughing. Michelle Yeoh is fantastic and deserving of all her praise and award buzz.

There is something so captivating about 60-year-old women performing incredible complex kung fu against one another. The brutality is superb and incredibly fun to watch. Another layer to the action is the actions our characters must perform to tape into their mulit-versal selves. These are crazy, vulgar, and some of the most shocking things I have seen on screen.

I've said I never need to hear the term "multiverse" again. This is an exception… As much as the final message is a simple one, there's so much going on here — given the infinite possibilities of infinite multi-verses — to keep the viewer entertained throughout the 140-minute runtime. Yes, the concept can devolve into a Family Guy bit of "RANDOM THING/PERSON interacts with RANDOM THING/PERSON for interest or comedic effect," but the plot, somehow, stays grounded enough to balance funny situations and endearing moments — I loved the "rock universe," while the "hotdog fingers universe" could've been stripped-down to a scene or two. Every character has to give a range because of the range of multiverses in which each character appears. Michelle Yeoh as our protag, Evelyn, is the star, but the whole Wang Family (Stephanie Hsu, Ke Huy Quan, James Hong), also deserves praise. Jamie Lee Curtis as Deirdre, an IRS Agent in whatever you call the starting-verse, is the perfect antagonist (and also friend, love interest, etc.). We all knew (yes, you're included in this) that her IRS trophies that adorned her administrative office resembled giant buttplugs — I appreciate that "The Daniels" followed the "Chekhov's Gun" rule in that regard. It's not the easiest to review, but I will say this, Everything Everywhere All at Once is the kind of movie that gives me hope. It's original, comprehensive in approach, but simple in message, fun, and funny. It can be enjoyed at home, but perhaps bolstered by a theater viewing. I love Swiss Army Man and didn't realize EEAaO was only their second full-feature collaboration. When I had been set in my thinking that anything original will only come from foreign filmmakers, I finally get to this. I hope it comes away with some hardware at the Oscars. There's also lots of Kung Fu.

In the competition for the Oscar this year, the highest number of nominations was won by "Everything Everywhere All at Once", which I did not think deserved any review, but since there is really no reasonable achievement in the offer for the award, here are a few words about it, and some attempt at analysis everything that will possibly happen to us at the assignment.

The theme of parallel worlds is not new either in science fiction or in the film industry. The revived interest is due to the influence of the late-phase Marvel movies. So, if this film wins some awards, it will be a kind of victory for Marvel, since they didn't manage to push their "Wakanda Forever", which should not be at all in this year's competition. By the way, it should be said that the nomination of Angela Bassett for supporting role is controversial, because no matter how good the actress is, the film for which she receives the award should still be good, which is not the case here. And Chadwick Boseman was a good actor, but no one thought of nominating him for the highly overrated first part of the "Black Panther" series.

What to say about "Everything..."? The film is technically excellent, the camera and direction are outstanding, the inspiring ways of filming deserve all the praise. But that would be all about it. Short cut shots, jumps from universe to universe, kaleidoscopes of colors and a variety of scenography, all of which would make it seem as if something is actually happening, cannot be a substitute for an overly thin script (if there was one at all). Anyway, the awards follow him in any case, because the film is sufficiently "woke" and feministic, and the actresses Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Lee Curtis were up to the task. When I first watched Everything Everywhere All at Once, I thought it was one of the best movies I've ever seen. But after rewatching it after some time, I am convinced that it is the best form of any storytelling I have ever come across. Granted, I haven't watched, read or played every movie/show/play, book or game ever created in the many languages that exist. But of the significant portion of my life I have spent experiencing stories and my subjective & biased parameters for what an exceptional form of storytelling should ideally be based on, I am certain that this movie is the best I've come across yet.

Why do I think that?

Because it combines the most investigated philosophical question of the purpose of life, the most complex metaphysical theory of multiverses and the most consistently prevalent emotions of hope & despair, all together, in 150 minutes that span almost every storytelling genre there is.

And it does this with a series of truly extraordinary & powerful acting performances, elegantly simple yet extremely compelling dialogues, absurdist yet coherent editing & transitions and one of the most narratively complementary cinematography ever.

Furthermore, the exceptionally intelligent use of various styles of humour, balanced with a metaphorical yet deeply compassionate use of relationships, to construct a narrative that - though may appear comically-absurd & entertaining on a casual first-watch - is actually so much more; being consistently deliberate, methodical & profound on a second viewing.

All this coalesces into a unique emotional journey - with an abundance of excellent humour - that inevitably transitions to a rollercoaster ride of hope crescendos & despair diminuendos, while offering convincing justifications for these ebbs and flows, concluding in an extremely cathartic & appropriate ending.

Everything Everywhere All at Once - as the title suggests - is truly a story about everything, everywhere, told all at once. It's the most conclusive story of existence. And as cliched and inaccurate its ultimate moral may seem, it ingeniously conveys it in the single most hopeful & captivating manner possible.

And that's why it is the best form of any storytelling I have ever come across.

Packed to the brim with big ideas, challenging cinematography, uproarious laughs, and surprising action Everything Everywhere All at Once is a genre-less thrill ride that proves itself as one of the year's best films. The movie begins simply enough: a Chinese immigrant family who owns a laundromat gets audited by the IRS for overextending the definition of the phrase "write-off." When they have to go speak with an IRS agent (played magnificently by the great Jamie Lee Curtis) the result is anything but simple. Evelyn Wang, the family's matriarch (played by the exceptional Michelle Yeoh) is approached by a different version of her husband, Waymond (Ke Huy Quan). This version is from an alternate reality and he warns that there is a multiversal force that threatens the existence of every reality and that this version of Evelyn Wang is the secret to defeating this ominous, evil force. This threat turns out to be a version of Evelyn's daughter, Joy (played by the scene-stealing Stephanie Hsu), who is capable of tapping into other versions of herself in order to borrow their skills to ensure that her abilities are limitless. What results is a surprisingly intimate look into family, potential, and self-worth against the backdrop of infinity. It's a film that defies any sort of pigeonhole; viewers will laugh throughout, be amazed at the choreography of the fight scenes, and will even cry when the total weight of everything starts to be addressed. Everything Everywhere All at Once is a movie who's title can be believed, it's a visual spectacle that is sure to stick with you well after the credits roll. It's a thematically rich tapestry that proves just how big a single film can really be, I can't wait to watch it again.

I get both the good and the bad reviews for this movie. This movie is hard to understand and had a complex, almost ridiculous plot line. It uses things like the multiverse and martial arts to help tell the story, which I don't think it needed, but it was what the screenwriter and the director wanted to use, possibly to make this a unique premise, something never really tried before - though in different ways it has been done in other movies to different extents. The basic gist of the story is a mother who is trying to connect with her husband and her daughter, and how in all the different universes they find that connection, and where they lose also lose their connections to each other. It is also a very philosophical movie, touching upon the absurdity of life and our humanity. It takes awhile in the movie to get to that point. A Pat-Oh_Meter Review

First off, the title should be modified to say, "Everything, Everywhere, All at Once, Over and Over, and Way too Long." Although the run time is only two hours and 19 minutes, the repetitive nature of the film's multiverse, mad-cap action left me wishing the darn thing would end.

Sad to say, since my husband and I had looked forward to seeing this one. The performances were great. The multiverse concept intriguing. The fast-paced scenes and elaborate settings were amazing. My gosh, the shooting script must have been 400 pages.

But the point of this film, which is disguised as a sci-fi comedy, is essentially a dysfunctional family coming together to forgive. Plot-wise, that's about it, although the filmmakers kept hammering lines like "nothing matters" and "be kind" and "we're all small and stupid" and even the "F" word all by itself on screen for us to treasure. 

A mature Michelle Yeoh stars as the overwhelmed Evelyn Wang who's in tax trouble with IRS, divorce trouble with her long-suffering husband, and relationship trouble with her daughter. Yeoh deserves an Oscar for her exceptional performance as a woman who discovers her true powers.

Jamie Lee Curtis camps through the role of a frustrated IRS agent and might take home a trophy for best supporting actress. Stephanie Hsu manages not to mess up her dual roles as Evelyn's lesbian daughter and some sort of evil goddess called Juba. The male actors were all fine in their roles.

But for some reason, other than when Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Lee Curtis were on-screen, I found myself bored with the film's existential platitudes and truly wanted it to end. Okay, so I at least found the spinning bagel funny. (I won't explain.)

The Academy's Oscar "representation" requisites were fulfilled by having a mostly Asian cast, a female lead, a disabled father, and several gay-girl scenes. You might find it interesting to review the Academy's recent "representation guidelines," which in my opine are over the top. However, they do explain why you're now seeing so many gay-girl scenes in films.

The most disposable scenes were two rocks in the desert discussing the futility of their existence. Heck, cutting that scenario might have reduced the run time by at least 10 minutes. Truly: was this "Waiting for Godot" in rock form? I got the feeling those scenes were added in post by someone who thought using rocks was a brilliant idea.

Forgive me for being either too jaded or over-lit-majored or envious of the filmmaker's amazing ability to put this thing together and win an Oscar, but the Pat-Oh-Meter gives this highly rated, highly touted film only 3.5 out of five stars.

Call me old-fashioned, but originality in film should include creativity in what words emanate from the actors' mouths—and especially what emotions those words instill in the audience. A great film should not be an endless melange of bizarre, creative, and entertaining scenes.

As "Everything Everywhere All at Once" (2022 release; 139 min.) opens, we are introduced to Evelyn Quan, who along with her husband, runs a laundromat. At this point we are 10 minutes into the movie.

Couple of comment: this is the latest from writers-producers-directors Daniel Kwam and Daniel Scheineret (a/k/a "the Danierls"). This is only their second feature length movie, after 2016's critically acclaimed "Swiss Army Man". Like that movie, in "Everything Everywhere All at Once" they bring a highly original premise and story line. Frankly, the plot is so off kilter that it doesn't even make any sense, nor need it be. Instead, one simply sits back and enjoys whatever is unfolding on the screen. Michelle Yeoh is outstanding as Evelyn. I didn't realize that the IRS auditor is played by Jamie Lee Curtis until the credits rolled. I don't know if others felt the same, but I felt a bit overwhelmed, if npot exhausted, by it all and I watched the entire movie over two equal parts on consecutive evenings. That does not mean that I didn't like the movie, let me be clear.

"Everything Everywhere All at Once" was an unexpected box office hit during its US theatrical run that started last Spring, For whatever reason I just didn't feel drawn to it. Then earlier this week, it gathered an amazing 11 Oscar nominations, more than any other film, and I told myself I really needed to find out what the buzz was all about. I watched the film earlier this week (it's streaming on Showtime). Glad I did. If you are in the mood for truly something very different and uniquely original, I'd readily suggest you check this out, and draw your own conclusion.

The film is a sly parody of the Marvel Cinematic Universe's (MCU) "What If" series in its exploration of alternate realities, but quickly switches tracks to ground the narrative and its characters in our reality to explore many themes that are close to home. Chief of those themes is the importance of priorities, with filmmakers writing a good chunk of Evelyn's dialogue to emphasize her desperation on keeping the family business afloat while facing the consequences of her decisions. This is further explored in the early flashback scenes of Evelyn's and Waymond's relationship, the birth of their family business, and the birth of their daughter.

Throughout the film, filmmakers also allude to the importance of acceptance. We see this play out with Evelyn and her father, tiptoeing around the topic of her daughter dating another woman. This theme is also echoed by the constant shift in Waymond's personality, who alternates between his present non-masculine self, and his alternate reality personality who is a confident and skilled fighter, whom Evelyn falls deep in love with. The biggest thing Evelyn had to come to terms with throughout the film was accepting that she was burned out, that she couldn't shoulder all the family's responsibility on her own, and that it was okay for her to ask for help.

This leads to the other theme that was explored in the film - the strength to rely on others. Throughout the film, we see the effects of Evelyn shouldering everything on her own. We see everything around her starting to crumble, figuratively and literally. This eventually leads to her falling apart, not knowing what to do. These scenes contrast drastically with the final few scenes of the film where we see Evelyn happy, having those weights lifted from her shoulders.

One other theme that filmmakers chose to explore with this reality-bending film is the importance of facing reality. This is seen throughout the movie with the intercut scenes of the other realities, which Evelyn slowly begins running away to when things become too overwhelming for her. Eventually, with those realities beginning to fold into her own, she is forced to return to her reality to address what she has done and what she has to do.

This film is a wonderful exploration of both reality and alternate realities. Every scene is meaningful and well-paced, with a great blend of well-choreographed and whimsical action scenes. Despite being conceptually brilliant, the film's villain is plagued by the "MCU villain" problem, being two-dimensional in portrayal and dialog. Filmmakers had a golden egg in their hands with the concept of the film's big bad but failed to leverage more on her backstory to make her more relatable, especially to younger teenage audiences who could see themselves in the villain's shoes. What made it worse was the overwhelming contrast between the main character and the villain of the film, with the main character's performance and dialog outshining that of the villain. Nevertheless, the heart of the story remains clear and simple for audiences of most age groups to understand and appreciate. With a personal rating of 4.5/5, Everything Everywhere All at Once is a must-watch film for parents and teenagers alike, especially in theaters with the right audio and video formats.

There is a rumor that they wanted Jackie Chan at first. With that knowledge, you can see how this character was almost tailor-made for him; he would have been glorious, and he could probably spice up those low-budget martial arts scenes they had. However, on the opposite end of the spectrum from Michelle is Ke Huy Quan. He is just marvelous and, in my view, carried the movie. In the end, the glitzy editing and too much stuff being thrown on screen dilute the movie. Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (A.K.A Daniels) bring audiences a fascinating film about a Chinese immigrant who becomes entangled in a multiverse-spanning adventure after trying to do her taxes. BAFTA nominee Michelle Yeoh stars alongside Stephanie Hsu, Ke Huy Quan, James Hong, and Jamie Lee Curtis in one of 2022's most exciting films.

‘Everything Everywhere All at Once' follows Evelyn Wang (Michelle Yeoh), an overworked Chinese immigrant who runs a laundromat with her husband Waymond, while also dealing with the strained relationship she has with her daughter and her judgemental father. Amid juggling her personal issues, Evelyn must attend a meeting with the IRS to discuss her business' web of finances. However, what occurs during this meeting will change the course of Evelyn's life forever, taking her on a mammoth journey across the multi-verse that makes for one of A24's craziest films.

Even though ‘Everything Everywhere All at Once' is a film that features wacky, unpredictable action, Daniel Kwan and Daniel Schienert direct a film that, despite its crazy fight sequences is packed topfull of complex emotion. The directing duo bring audiences a film that manages to inject powerful emotions into some of the wackiest scenarios you'll ever see. Perhaps the film's ability to balance heart-wrenching sentiment, outrageous comedy and erratic action is what makes it such a unique film, even by A24's boundary-pushing standards. ‘Everything Everywhere All at Once' does carry a hefty runtime with its daring storyline, coming in at 139 minutes, even longer than this year's other multi-versal event, Sam Raimi's ‘Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness' which is only 126 minutes. However, unlike its Marvel counterpart, it audiences a more thorough insight into the world's many universes. We get to see universes where Evelyn (Yeoh) takes on careers like being a professional singer, acting and a Teppanyaki chef, as well as worlds where humanity evolved to have hot-dog fingers or places where life was never born, thus resulting in Joy (Hsu) and Evelyn taking on the form of rocks. This scene between Evelyn and Joy surprises viewers who will end up crying at two rocks engaging in a subtitled conversation about the complexity of life.

Michelle Yeoh and Stephanie Hsu both give magnificent performances and by the end of the film audiences will be excited for their next outing together, which as of May 2022, the pair have both been announced to star in the new Disney+ series ‘American Born Chinese'. Hsu's performance as both versions of Joy make you feel like you're watching two vastly different actors and makes for performance you can't draw yourself away from. Ke Huy Quan also delivers a brilliant turn as both versions of Waymond, one as a feeble and wimpy version of Evelyn's husband and the other as a skilled fighter and multi-verse traveller. However, the highlight of both Quan and Yeoh's performances comes towards the end of the film in which alternate versions of Waymond and Evelyn discuss what could've been in a scene that emanates films from acclaimed director Wong Kar Wai. Jamie Lee Curtis delivers a hilarious performance as Deidre and the alternate versions of the mundane IRS officer

Audiences are thrown in for an emotional rollercoaster when they sit down to watch ‘Everything Everywhere All at Once', dealing with themes of acceptance, divorce, love, and the complexity of mother/daughter relationships. So not only does the film deliver on it's promise of an ‘insane adventure', but also tugs at your heartstrings. The film is filled with top-notch craftsmanship, ranging from clever editing that elevates the project to another level and an impressive screenplay from Scheinert and Kwan. This is a film that isn't afraid to be unapologetically silly or ridiculous, and perhaps that's what makes is such a special film.

‘Everything Everywhere All at Once' is a film that puts a wacky and refreshingly unique spin on the idea of a multiverse, made popular by Marvel's ever-growing universe of films. Directing duo Daniels create a film that not only entertains with it's interesting and thought-provoking story, but also with its impressive technical factors and performances that will hopefully make it a contender in the 2022/23 awards season. The film joins the ranks of some of A24's best films, sitting on the same shelf as films like Greta Gerwig's 2017 coming-of-age film ‘Lady Bird', Mike Mills drama ‘C'mon C'mon and Ari Aster's terrifying horror ‘Midsommar'. Taking its audiences on a wild ride across the multiverse, ‘Everything Everywhere All at Once' takes its spot as one of 2022's best films already and brings a ground-breaking story to audiences across the world.
