ENGLISH REVIEW
Everything Everywhere All at Once is a movie that is best experienced without knowing too much about it. In short, it follows a Chinese immigrant family dealing with tax issues and relationship problems, but it's so much more than that. The movie is a unique blend of originality, creativity, heart, and absurdity, with Michelle Yeoh's Evelyn and her daughter Joy (played by Hsu) at the center of the story. The relationship between Evelyn and Joy drives the narrative through its multiverse-spanning journey, with help from other characters like Waymond, Gong Gong, and Deirdre. Yeoh shines in her role as she portrays multiple versions of herself in an action-packed and emotionally charged performance. The movie is filled with weird and wonderful characters, situations, and lifestyles as the Daniels (the filmmakers) fully embrace the madness of the concept. Despite the absurdity, the movie never loses sight of the importance of family and provides a deep look at generational trauma, existentialism, and identity. The movie also takes the audience on an emotional journey, culminating in a tear-inducing finale. It's a truly impressive feat given the eccentric and outlandish nature of the movie, and in a time where audiences are craving originality, Everything Everywhere All at Once delivers with a fearless and nonconformist approach. It's a cinematic maverick that's bonkers, chaotic, and wild – a rare treat.

Approaching this kind of movie can be really complicated, and not just because they're far distant from the Hollywood routine, but also because they are quite difficult to portray and convey on paper. Indeed, watching this movie only one time isn't enough to understand it all and to appreciate all the incredible visual elements, made more from make up and costume design than from CGI, the Daniels, at their second work together, put on screen in this "absurdist comedy-drama film". A chaos of genres, fights, kung-fu, side universes and emotions that leaves the spectator astonished and surprised. If a comparison can be made, EEAAO it has reminded me of "The Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind",  with more bravery and weirdness: in the 2004 Carrey-Winslet movie, they played with different level of memories, while here Michelle Yeoh and He Huy Quan moves through different temporal lines. A multiverse of messy and quirky madness (explored like never before, neither in the Avengers saga) swallows a chinese family who is going to file a tax return at the IRS centre for their coin-operated laundromat service. These two lines can even briefly sum up the plot but they aren't able to widely describe what actually happen in the movie because, like I said before, a complete description could have not been done and, even if I've tried, I've probably used not just two lines, but two hundred. The family is composed by Evelyn Quan Wang (Michelle Yeoh), married to Waymond Wang (He Huy Quan), who is trying to talk about divorce papers with her, their daughter Joy (Stephanie Hsu), who is having a relationship with Becky (that has been hidden by Gong Gong), and Gong Gong, Evelyn's father (James Hong), who has moved from China to celebrate new chinese year'. While they're talking with tax inspector Deirdre Beaubeirdre (Jamie Lee Curtis), Waymond's soul is uncounsciously replaced with his Alpha version, from another universe: he starts to explain to a terrified Evelyn that many universes exists over the one in which they're living and that his world is threated by Joy's evil version, Jobu Tupaki. From that moment, Evelyn will become more and more aware of her powers and will do whatever she can to save the multiverse. Like Nolan's Interstellar, this movie uses a world-saving story like a ram's head in order to talk of human relations: this movie indeed explores the life of an immigrant (and a woman) to tell the difficulties we everyday face,  the struggles and stress that affect us everyday and everywhere. It's a movie about a husband who never finds the right moment to say to his wife: "I want to divorce"; it's a story about a troubled mother-daughter relation, that mixes grief, disappointment, disillusion and harshness; about a mother that refuses to accept her daughter for what she actually is. Through a superb montage that doesn't leave any spaces to relax, EEAAO never loses his pace and gifts the world of cinema to a unique and crazy piece, capable of winning 7 Oscars in the 2023 edition by destroying Field's "Tar" and Mcdonagh's "The Banshess of Inisherin". Remarkable all Curtis's scenes (first Oscar for her). 
Extra: this movie it has been produced by the Daniels with the Russo brothers and A24: a detail that answers the deja-vu sensation that affected many MCU addicted and fans. And, furthermore, with A24 it traces a thread with the indie world.

What a fantastic return-to-the-big-screen vehicle for the talented Ke Huy Quan, another amazing showcase of Michelle Yeoh's endless talent, and a great cameo role for Jamie Lee Curtis. Stephanie Hsu ate up scenery in her endless stream of wildly fashionable costumes and dry delivery as the insidious yet oddly likable Jobu Tupaki. 

Everything, Everywhere, All At Once effectively delivered a ridiculous amount of ideas and visuals compacted into a refreshing theme that was both enlightening and heartwarming. It seemed to be saying; 'Your limitless potential is only buried under your fear of being out of the ordinary' while also pairing it with the power of kindness.  It's an important message in a very real era of division, distrust, and blind animosity amplified by the power of social media.

The best part of this film is the opening shot where we witness a family, laughing and jumping up and down as they watch something, through a mirror on the wall, paired by some clever chords from Son Lux's overall meh score. Beyond that opening shot though, is a VERY meh movie. The idea of this film is incredibly creative and very ambitious. To the editor for splicing together so many multiverse shots and to the Daniels for writing and directing said shots, I commend them. However, to do a multiverse film and simultaneously address the meaning of life in a profound way…I don't think they quite pulled it off. The character of Joy represents our modern society and every classic young adult today that feels hopeless and doesn't have another deep thought afterward. This is supposedly a film about a mother and daughter who can't quite understand each other or love one another well. To properly resolve such a broken relationship, the emotional scene at the end would sound something like this: Evelyn saying, "I'm sorry. I know that you hate your life and that things are hard. I don't want that for you. I love you. We can make this relationship work and try to help each other out," with Joy replying, "I love you too, mom. And I'm sorry for everything before. Yes, let's do this. Let's make this work." Instead, we get Evelyn saying, "We can do whatever we want. Nothing matters," with Joy replying, "This is so embarrassing." This is not a character arc where flaws are conquered and a compromise is made between two colliding personalities. This is simply a brief addressing of an existing pain, followed by a sarcastic ignoring of it. I also do not understand the hype over the acting. Don't get me wrong, Ke Huy Quan plays his part perfectly, is quite endearing, and the best character in the film. However, his role is not a hard one to play nor demanding of an Oscar. Stephanie Hsu plays her part very well and has the most depth to her character, but the character is poorly written, over-ridden with attitude and spite and robbed of the sympathy and empathy that would make an audience root for her. Michelle Yeoh does not stun in a complex, awe-inspiring role. She does just fine in the role of a mom who gets to be a comic-book hero for a day. And Jamie Lee Curtis does not transform herself into a SAG-award-winning IRS agent. She simply is her funny, goofy Jamie Lee Curtis self making us laugh because she's Jamie Lee Curtis. Yes, the comedic elements of this movie and some of the jokes and gags that come around are hilarious and quite clever. But, if Ke Huy Quan needed me to commit an impossibility to travel to an alternate universe, for me, it would not be to confess my love for Jamie Lee Curtis or to stick a cone up my ass, but to say with confidence that Everything Everywhere All At Once is the best picture of the year.

This masterpiece is all about everything happening everywhere, just like the title. And I assure you that you will feel the same way as I do when you watch it. So there will be a question about what is even "everything" to start with. Everything is about your life and those people who you are surrounded with. This movie may be fictional by the inclusion of a multiverse but the depiction of underlying philosophical meaning about the realistic view of family issues, life choices, and all the possibilities we could create from small insignificant decisions in our daily lives reflect and wonder about our lives a lot. The whole plot itself takes place in the multiverse which might be something confusing when people who are unfamiliar with the concept hear that but surprisingly it is very simple to comprehend the whole plot. 

It will give you a tremendous amount of different emotions, some of them which you might not have even experienced before. At least, it was that way for me. Many types of comedy also take place in the plot frequently and all of them are fantastic and in perfect timing. Despite having so many funny and ridiculous scenes, the plot itself is very serious to the point everyone can relate to either characters or situations in their lives such as the scenes when the movie depicted the young couple making "wrong" choices in this universe, the parenthood focusing on both the perspective of the wife (Evelyn)  and the husband (Waymond), their teenage daughter (Joy)'s problems concerning her life choices being unaccepted by her mother, ruined and shattered hopes from a young couple,  their business situations, the typical dead romance between the long-married couple (especially Asian couples), and many other characters' plots and viewpoints.


There are no villains in this movie. At the first glance, you might probably think (as it is stereotyped) of the mysterious character who seems to have bad intentions toward the universe, Jobu Tupaki (Joy) as the villainess. But if you can truly apprehend the way she becomes who she is, her actions are not justifiable but are understandable. Then, her mother would be the one you would want to blame for making Joy the way she is. But turns out, that is also not the case as everyone always wants the best for themselves or their loved ones. Her mother's action is also understandable but not justifiable. So in short, either her father, her grandfather and his organization, her mother, herself and everyone and every version of them in different universes cannot be blamed as it is going in a circle, and not one person can be blamed for one exact cause. 

Last of all, "Nothing matters", the main concept of this movie. This line mentioned by Jobu Tupaki(Joy) is a very simple yet powerful line for everyone everywhere it also shows her belief in one of the most famous philosophical branches called Nihilism. She tried to end the whole multiverse and universes by sucking everything into the giant bagel with her superpowers because nothing really matters to her anymore. But the fact that she wanted to end it together with her mother from the far multiverse shows that someone still matters to her and if we think carefully about Joy, she is doing all these things because of the concept of "nothing matters" matters to her. And yes it actually feels nice to think that way because if nothing matters, all the pain and guilt we feel from nothing of our lives go away as it is stated by Jobu Tupaki. But on the contrary and concluding from the ending and Evelyn's fighting scene against her daughter to stop her from going into the bagel, we can say that because nothing really matters, it is our choice to decide what and who matters in our daily lives and give and try our best for them no matter whatever the hardship we may face. I think that everyone should watch this movie at least once in their lifetime. You will get an unbelievably amazing experience and feeling in the duration of these 2 hours.

I'm going to be blunt: This movie is like a bright speckled donut injected with some super stale bland bread and with a hollow core.

We get it. It's a story about a mother of a depressed, anxious suicidal young adult, but the treatment is so shallow that if you try to dive in you'll break something. 

Daughter: The writers never really get into the daughter and present her as a flapping conundrum for the mother. The writers see fit to laminate a layer of gay in the daughter as if somehow that helps support the daughter's feelings (offensive meter is ticking), but never really delve into the experience of being gay and they never show a moment of gayness in the film, they just slap a label on her, make her hold a girl's hand and the job is done. Instead they focus on presenting the daughter as a writhing ball of whimsical existential angst - and that's it.

On to the mother: Just a trope of a character. Maternal angst meets bored middle aged woman stuck in a rut. Yay.

Their relationship: They don't have one. It's just two shallow characters, one pulling away and the other trying to cling on, "SAVE" the other from themselves and neither really understanding the other. Hot tip for the writers: without you guys writing these characters as more than a window shop painting, you can't write true connection between them. How do you display human understanding between two characters if there's nothing for the audience to understand either?

The rest of the movie was shiny and silly. 

The shine: The shine was pretty. Lots of pretty things. They were shiny. They were well done. I liked them! But you can't watch 2:20 of shiny things alone… well I cant. Gummies aren't legal where I live.

The silly: The kind of silly people who wear Depends appreciate, but for everyone else it's like trying to share a meal with the same person after they've taken their evening Xanax.

I think the acting was phenomenal, and that the general storyline held a lot of promise and significance.  I believe they chose a heroine and a storyline in general which provided a lot of social commentary about modern American life, and the overwhelming nature of our capitalist culture and how it punishes minorities the most.  

Unfortunately, the film seems to lack an articulated or properly-maintained plot at points, and tries to juggle way too many different themes and directions at the same time to be comprehensible.  I was very frustrated by how often the plot took off ramps onto another theme or action scene, without fully developing and explaining what was going on (descriptively or symbolically) in the previous scenes.  I'm guessing this may have something to do with the average American's ever decreasing attention span and critical thinking skills, which seems to have negatively influenced Hollywood film directing over the years.  Regardless of the real reason behind these directing decisions, it made it very difficult to absorb the material at times.

I was also disappointed with the character development of Jobu Tupaki/Joy.  I never felt the audience got sufficient explanation or context behind /why/ she was so suicidal and hostile toward her mother, beyond some superficial information detailing typical parent/ teen child antagonism, or the story of split personalities due to too much multiverse switching.  Someone who is going through complex suffering and struggles to develop into that character deserves a comprehensive backstory and contextual interpretation.  Perhaps some of the explanations for her pain lie in inter-generational conflicts within Chinese American families, in which case that explanation may have been lost in cultural translation.  But I also think aspects of her backstory and character may have also just been poorly written.

Also, there are far too many kink and BDSM material to make me feel comfortable. Unless these BDSM scenes were poorly-developed attempts at satire, the film seemed to otherwise be promoting a culture that for many people is often one of out-of-control consumerism, exploitation, and abuse.  I get it, adding this material gives the illusion of adding prestige, exoticism, or 'intricacy' to a film.  That's often the effect BDSM references have on general audiences, since that culture is taken at face value as a 'rebellion against normalcy'.  Introducing BDSM themes out of context also has some kind of shock and awe effect, and can be injected in content that may not otherwise be sufficiently thought provoking.  But that's just it, the real value of this material is illusive, and putting motifs of kinky practices in film to substitute more powerful messages or ideas can't fool everyone.  That's not including how gross and disturbing a lot of the kink content was to begin with.

The academy should be ashamed of themselves because this choice seemed more of a racially biased move or political move, I can't put my finger on it but they definitely got that one wrong and missed an opportunity to give a premiere actress her flowers while she's still with us. I noticed that there's been criticism of the movie Wakanda Forever as there are many people in the United States, and across the world, that have a hard time grasping the idea of an elite African nation, on top of the food chain that, couple with the fact that the movie highlights some injustices on behalf of the white man. I get it, but let's take off our blinders and be real. Conversely, EEAAO is receiving positivity biased kudos due to the industry's recent infatuation with Asian inclusivity. And don't get me wrong, the actors in this movie are absolutely phenomenal and this is nothing against them, this is against the academy, this is against the biased critics. Yes, the movie is different and refreshing but that does not make it a better movie than some of its competing films.

This film was literally unwatchable for me. 

I got headaches from the audiovisual experience, but also from constantly rolling my eyes.

I almost never give up on a film, so I soldiered through this torturous assault on the senses, taking breaks every 30 minutes or so.

From the first minute, it starts out with people frantically rushing, tripping and talking over each other seemingly in fast-forward, constantly switching between English and Cantonese. First you think that this is intentional, so as to convey the chaotic situation, and once it is established, the pace and tone will settle down. Nope. This is the entire film. 

The film is a nonsensical mish-mash cacophony of frantic, hectic, hyper, non-stop dialog, noise, lights, people, and things. I understand that this is the point, and it's supposed to be Funny & Satirical & Smart & Weird & Sweet & Edgy & Silly & Serious & Meta.

However in my opinion it tries way, way too hard, and ultimately falls flat on its face in all its aspirations. At least the title is apt.

One of the most impressive aspects of the film is its visual style. The directors utilize an array of cinematic techniques, including animation, puppetry, and practical effects, to create a unique and mesmerizing visual experience. The cinematography is stunning, with vibrant colors and dynamic camera movements that keep the audience engaged throughout the film.

The performances are also outstanding, with each actor bringing a unique energy and charisma to their role. Yeoh delivers a powerful performance as the enigmatic Madame Wong, while Curtis is hilarious as a ruthless businesswoman who becomes embroiled in the chaos of Mei's mission.

But perhaps the most impressive aspect of "Everything Everywhere All at Once" is its storytelling. The film manages to balance multiple genres, including science fiction, action, comedy, and drama, with remarkable ease. The narrative is complex and engaging, and the filmmakers masterfully weave together the different threads of the story to create a satisfying and emotional conclusion.

Overall, "Everything Everywhere All at Once" is a remarkable piece of cinema that is sure to become a classic. With its stunning visuals, outstanding performances, and compelling storytelling, it stands out as one of the best films of all time. It's a must-see for anyone who appreciates bold, innovative filmmaking and a testament to the boundless potential of cinema as an art form.

First review I'm doing on Rotten Tomatoes!
I want to start of with saying that this movie is one of those movies you have to watch in one sitting and preferably on a big screen. To not have you wait for my honest feedback I'll give it now and then explain why. In all of the movies I have watched, enjoying everything from comedies to action films, sci-fi and dramas, this is absolutely the greatest masterpiece I have ever had the pleasure to watch. If I could, I would love to watch it for the first time again - such an emotional journey it takes one on.
I have to mention one thing to set your expectations straight: - do not go into this movie aching for a logical, realistic, planned through story to be told- if you do you'll be very disappointed. This is not like any other movie, this is a piece of film - the conglomerations of visuals and sound that produce tension and get the audiences attention. 
Befor watching this movie, I did not know why this movie won so many Oscar's, I was more pessimistic on the overall quality of the movie. The reason why i believe it's one of the greatest film artworks ever is because the absence of rationality and logic, of structured content and foreseeable behaviour allows the creation of feelings and a connection with the overall human emotions portrayed like no other movie has done. Because it does not make sense it feels so close to us. Most of what we experience, what we truly feel does not make sense - we can be angry but still love a person, we can have an abundance of things but still feel empty- unfulfilled. The movie creates so many different scenarios into which we can portray ourselves into, that it connects everybody to the plot ( hell I could not take my eyes off of the screen in the last 30 minutes). This gives everyone this (joy)ride of fast emotions that everyone has - the movie makes you feel happy, sad, disappointed, content, confused, orderly, scared all at the same time. The first half takes getting used to, but if you embrace the confusion, the chaos and watch the second half you'll have the absolute mesmerising experience of a wave of emotions coming over you, being captivated by the pleasure of what it feels like to be alive. Go and watch it!

It's extremely derivative (the plot is The Matrix) & there are too many references to other better films throughout as it jumps from 2001 Space Odyssey reference to Matrix reference to 'some other movie' reference.

Overall it's a very silly movie, that gets stuck between two conflicting tones (melodrama & slapstick comedy). Imagine the plot of The Matrix mixed with the tone of Scott Pilgrim. It's jocular tone doesn't match it's disconsolate themes (regret & nihilism). It contains strong components, but might've been better if treated more seriously, dramatically. Allow characters, themes, & actors to create tone so your fun can be earned through story. Instead it's forcefully directed like, "let's try to make it fun." Reminds me of the quote, "there's a difference between being smart & trying to be smart." So on one hand it's a somewhat fun movie, but on the other hand its fun is a contrivance.

Everything Everywhere All At Once is a genre-defying masterpiece that draws inspiration from a diverse range of cinematic influences, including martial arts epics like Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon and classics like 2001: A Space Odyssey. Directed by Dan Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, this film takes audiences on a  mind-bending journey through multiple dimensions, exploring complex themes of identity, existence, and the interconnectedness of all things.

Like Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon, Everything Everywhere All At Once features stunning martial arts choreography that blends seamlessly with the film's otherworldly visuals and intricate storytelling. And like 2001: A Space Odyssey, the film's exploration of the nature of existence and the limits of human consciousness is both profound and thought-provoking. With a powerhouse cast led by Michelle Yeoh, and stunning visuals that transport viewers to worlds beyond their wildest imagination, Everything Everywhere All At Once is a true cinematic triumph that pushes the boundaries of storytelling and captivates audiences from start to finish.

At over two hours long, Everything Everywhere All At Once is certainly an ambitious and sprawling film. However, the length is necessary to fully explore the film's complex themes and allow the story to unfold in a way that feels organic and satisfying. While plenty of viewers find the length of the film to be a challenge, it is ultimately a testament to the filmmakers' commitment to telling a truly epic and immersive story. So just be prepared, ready, set, go.

On the surface, this movie is about the multiverse, but it's not really. This is actually about mental health that comes from stress from being overworked and underappreciated, but there is a deeper aspect that is explored in greater detail later on, which is that the mother doesn't really accept that her daughter is gay. While she says she is okay with it, she isn't really, and the mental breakdown that the mother goes through is actually because she loves her daughter but because her daughter is gay it is impacting on the strength of their relationship and making them enemies when they should be friends. It is from the perspective of the mentally unwell mother, and it is done in a superhero-like way, akin to Spiderman into the Spiderverse, and all of the multiverse things that so many American superhero comics like to explore, especially Marvel, and perhaps the woman likes Marvel comics. It is quite transparent from the start what is going on, but it might trick some viewers, and hence it is a movie that can work in at least two ways at once, which is brilliant. You can quite happily take it literally, as if these things are really going on, the multiverse is real, and this is a superhero movie, or you can take it at a deeper level, about a mother's mental breakdown due to her inability to truly accept her daughter's homosexuality. In this way, it is one of the better LGBT movies in explaining the topics, as there are undoubtedly a lot of parents who say that they accept it because they love their children but they really don't because they don't like homosexuality. This was excused by the Chinese culture, but it can be applied more generally than that. It can probably be applied in other ways too. My biggest negative was the switching of languages from Chinese to English and back again, sometimes mid-sentence. While there were subtitles come up, it broke the feel of the movie, and I felt like to truly understand and appreciate it properly you had to speak both Chinese and English and probably also you had to be culturally Chinese. I felt a bit like a foreigner looking in and never truly understanding it. That is the only fault I have with it. I gave it 9/10

Everything Everywhere All At Once is a brilliant film. Cinema is so not dead! This film was an excellent commentary on the contrast between the Chinese mom, who is stereotypically closed off, unaffectionate, controlling and overall just always at conflict with her Americanized daughter. Who is also attracted to women, something that her mother is unable to understand. One of my favorite things about this film is how it happened throughout many different universes and timelines, many different worlds, and many different stories of the same people. Even a few stories where they are inanimate objects (the piñatas, drawings, and the rocks). But the story started, and ended, in the same day and universe. Throughout the film, much like in the film "About Time", there was a sense that everything is so fragile. Life is so fragile, every little thing can destroy a whole universe. It is shown by how Jobu Tupaki has been able to make a lot of universes a dystopia, and when Evelyn acquires skills from different universes, we also get to see how she messes up the lives of the different Evelyn's she comes in contact with. The film allows us for a second to ask ourselves if we are seeing the demise of Evelyn into another Jobu Tupaki (something that seems to hint at one of the main themes of the film - generational trauma). But then, the film immediately grabs our attention away from that question and distracts us with a crazy fight scene. When the film comes to its end, we get a glimpse of how all these conflicts are resolved. We also see how the conflict in Evelyn's universe is resolved. Even after all the universes she has traveled to. After not showing up for her tax audit, cursing out her tax auditor, picking up a baseball bat and shattering a window right behind her, AND ending up being handcuffed to a chair. Waymond is then able to resolve this whole conflict, letting Evelyn free and resolve her conflict with Joy. Another thing I loved is the amount of allusions to different films. Specifically to 2001: A Space Odyssey, and different works of Wong Kar Wai. The film was alluding to In The Mood For Love, in ITMFL, Chow asks Su li to join him in Singapore, to which she declines. The same thing happens in EEAAO, in that universe, Evelyn declines the offer of Waymond to join him in moving to the US. Everything Everywhere All At Once deals with human themes like familial love and feeling important in an enticing and unique way, its multiversal setting allowing for a unique approach to emphasizing the characters' feelings. Of course, a caveat to this is that the concept of the multiverse is often difficult to explain. However, the film manages to do so somewhat easily, as Alpha Waymound's explanation makes sense but is also delivered during tense moments, making the audience pay attention instead of losing focus as long exposition often does. Our main protagonist, Evelyn, is also thrust into the multiverse just as we are, allowing us to learn alongside her instead of simply throwing us into the deep end. However, there are some things that make the plot hard to follow, with the antagonist, Jobu Tupaki, being particularly vague in the beginning. For example, while it does imply that she can destroy the multiverse, it is difficult to believe when the protagonist force, the Alpha dimension, doesn't know much either. There is no connection as to why Tupaki is such a threat, with Alpha Waymound simply telling us that she is. Even towards the end, when Tupaki describes her machine, the bagel, there isn't much explanation for why we should fear it, with the only thing being Waymound's explanation half an hour earlier. While this is a convention of the Magical Realism genre, with the extraordinary elements being unexplained to appear normal, the film goes through great effort to explain everything else, such as how people can cross and manipulate the multiverse. Because of the previous explanations, the vagueness behind the supposedly deadly bagel machine is very apparent. Simultaneously, Tupaki's actions aren't very clear. Before attempting to destroy the multiverse, she explains that she was looking for someone, Evelyn, to share her power and help her out of her crisis. However, Jobu Tupaki doesn't seem to make any effort to "look for her," as it is the Alpha dimension who initially contacts Evelyn and gets the story going in the first place. At the end of the day, however, these problems aren't that noticeable during the course of the film. The dynamic between Evelyn and Tupaki, mother and daughter, is quite riveting. One might find themselves sobbing at the end of the film. Additionally, there are subtle gags here and there that keep the tone somewhat happy and refreshing despite the serious subject matter. Of course, the acting gets the job done, with Ke Huy Quan being particularly excellent in the innocence his character is supposed to represent. With Michelle Yeoh, she perfectly captures the confusion one would experience being thrust into the multiverse, allowing the audience to project themselves onto her as they ride through the story. All in all, Everything Everywhere All At Once, despite its minor flaws, is definitely an experience worth watching.

Overall, I really enjoyed Everything Everywhere All at Once, a movie that focuses on the struggles that a immigrant family have connecting with each other and reconciling their differences, and how a inter-universal conflict leads to them having to confront their problems by rejecting nihilism in favor of finding meaning in their relationships and their love for each other. Although the movie say so many things, at its core the message of this movie is, as far as I can tell, that one ought not to try to find meaning in their successes and failures or in the actions of others because all those things are inherently meaningless, but should instead find meaning in their relationships with others and the love they hold for them. This message is beautifully illustrated in the relationship between the main cast, Evelyn Quan-Wang, her husband Waymond, and their daughter Joy. The main conflict of the movie is centered around Evelyn trying to stop a version of Joy from another universe, who broke under the pressure of "her" Evelyn's expectations of her and gave into nihilism, from destroying the multiverse and herself. This conflict is a great extension of the message that one should not find successes or failures in another. The alternate Joy, Jobu Tupaki, was constantly pressured by Evelyn to perform, due to Evelyn deriving her worth from Jobu's successes, which is what led to Jobu snapping. This is summarized perfectly by a quote from the movie, said by Evelyn's father, "In my universe, you pushed your own daughter too hard until you broke her. You. You created Jobu Tupaki." This summarizes why one should not derive their meaning from others, it leads to you having expectations of them, which can adversely affect your relationship with them. The conflict also addresses Jobu's beliefs. Jobu, who is able to experience all versions of her existence in every universe, believes that because everything that can or will happen has happened in some other universe none of your actions or decisions matter, and that nothing matters in life. This is why she plans to "end her existence," commit suicide in other words, by entering the Everything Bagel. Jobu's sentiment can be explained by the a quote from the movie that claims humans are "all small & stupid," which continues to refer to life as "A big FUCKING joke." However, the film also rejects Jobu's view, and posits an answer in the form of Waymond, who agrees with the sentiment that life is confusing and nothing seems to matter, it's possible to find meaning in just being happy and kind, and in the people around you, not in the things you do or achieved. Encapsulated by the quote where an alternate, extremely successful, version of him tells Evelyn that "In another life, I would have really liked just doing laundry and taxes with you." It resolves the conflict by answering the questions both Evelyn and Jobu ask. It both shows Jobu that there is meaning in life, found in your relationships with others and the little things in everyday life, and shows Evelyn where to derive her meaning from instead of her own success or the success of others. As someone who has struggled with finding meaning in my own life, I found this message to be very inspiring, and uplifting. While I do believe that, at times, the movie went overboard with how absurd it made some of the alternate universes Evelyn visits to stop Jobu, I don't really have much to criticize in the film beyond that, which is why I give it 4.5 stars.

EEAAO is a gut-wrenching movie that every daughter should watch once in their life. The film follows Evelyn, a hardworking woman who immigrated to America to pursue a new life with her love, Waymond. They both run a laundromat and raise their daughter Joy who resents and loves her mother at the same time. Evelyn holds Joy back by not fully accepting Joy for her self-expression that she conveys through her queerness, clothing, etc. Right from the start of the film this love-hate dynamic between mother and daughter is established when Evelyn tells her father, Gong Gong, that Joy's girlfriend, Becky, is just her "friend." Joy is tired of her mother ignoring who she is, and experiences a lot of sadness as a result. However, Joy doesn't like expressing this openly to her mother because she knows all the struggles that Evelyn had to deal with growing up, like Gong Gong abandoning Evelyn when she chose to marry Waymond. This perpetuates the generational trauma both Evelyn and Joy face as they both do not openly express their true emotions. The film captures this anguish very well. For example, right in the beginning of the film after Evelyn lies to Gong Gong and says that Joy's girlfriend is actually her "very good friend," Joy goes to leave her family's laundromat. After taking care of a customer, Evelyn runs out to Joy to, as what the audience can infer, apologize for calling Becky a "friend". However, Evelyn can't find the courage to apologize and instead tells Joy that she is "getting fat". In the following shots we see Joy crying in her car once she is out of site of her mother and Evelyn with a troubled expression as she helps Gong Gong up some stairs. They both are tearing each other up from the inside but don't have the courage to admit it. This film does really well with having the unsaid words between Evelyn and Joy be clear to the audience. Like how Evelyn obviously wanted to say something personal to Joy before calling her "fat."
	Something that I wish was expanded on in the film was Joy's perspective. We see a lot on Jobu Tupaki, but not much of the Joy we are introduced to in the beginning. If this perspective was added, a deeper connection between the younger generation and the audience could have been found between Joy and the audience. A lot of Gen-Z, haven grown up in a world that preaches mental health awareness, know about generational trauma and why their parents may not feel comfortable talking about certain topics such as queerness. Therefore, having Joy's perspective would be key to bringing light to a wider audience the struggle the younger generation has to breaking their families generational curses whilst still trying not to hurt their parents feelings.
To end, I'll touch on some quotes that stuck with me:
"In another life, I would have really liked just doing laundry and taxes with you." - Waymond (talking to Movie Star Evelyn).
This quote always sticks out to me because it shows how whilst you may be having the worst day, or, as Alpha Waymond would put it, "living your worst you," simply your relationship to someone else can mean the world to them. It is quite touching because it reminds me of the people that I hold dear to me and how much of an impact they have made on my life. That simply being able to spend time sitting quietly with my family, even if doing separate things, is when I'm at my happiest. Even if life never becomes something grandeur, simply "doing laundry and taxes" with someone can becomes your best you if you allow it to be.
"Let her finish." - Joy (at the end of the film when she tells Waymond to let Evelyn finish her Joy complaint speech.)
I like these three words a lot because they conceptualize the relationship between Evelyn and Joy. They rarely ever say their true emotions towards each other so that when they do, it means everything to listen to them. Even though her mother's words may be hurting her, Joy quickly tells her dad to not interject. Sometimes when hurting each other feelings, the stronger and more loving they come out.

While the main theme of this movie "the importance of familial connection and love" has been told time and time again, EEAAO is a beautiful rendition of this idea. Michelle Yeoh deserved everything she got for this role, as did Ke Huy Quan. Stephanie Hso is soon to be one of the greatest actors of her generation mark my words.  So glad this won best movie. Absolutely mind-boggling and truthful.

The pitch of a "multiverse movie" may evoke many emotions to those deciding whether to watch this film. It may feel corny, cliché, or just plain uninteresting. But the audience will quickly be surprised as "Everything Everywhere All at Once" blows all preconceived notions away and leaves them with an astonishingly profound, unapologetically silly, and fearlessly original piece that will make them laugh, cry, and think all within its well-used 140-minute runtime.

A magnificent Michelle Yeoh stars as overworked laundromat owner and immigrant mother Evelyn Wang, who, while being audited by the IRS's Deirdre (an always worthwhile Jamie Lee Curtis) and left by her husband Waymond (a triumphant return from Ke Huy Quan), quickly realizes things are not what they seem, and that in fact, she must save the world from a nihilist maniac in the form of her daughter (the slick and stylish Stephanie Hsu). Quickly and unflinchingly bombarded with hot dog fingers, kung fu moves (in a lovely homage to Yeoh herself), movie stardom, a raccoon as Ratatouille, love, and loss, she soon realizes, as she's faced with the absurdness of the multiverse and of life itself around her, that what she's really needed has been in front of her all along.

"Everything Everywhere All at Once" gracefully flicks between fast-paced action, rapid-fire silliness, and tear-jerking drama, and while it sounds overwhelming, the Daniels' superb direction makes sure the audience is always satisfied. The cinematography, costume design, score, and set pieces all complement the story's tremendous theme, aided by metaphors that sound as ridiculous as googly-eyed rocks and an everything bagel that actually has everything on it, but end up representing so much more.

There's no way around it: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" is a masterpiece.

The comedy just didn't land for me in this movie, and the extreme absurdity of the attempted comedy then made it hard to take the other portions more seriously. There were some interesting moments in the family drama and during the initial exploration of the multiverses. The acting was also quite good, so I give it 2 stars.

The humor struck me as too aggressively silly and absurd, like those old Jim Carrey or Chris Farley movies I watched as a teen back in the '90's. It just seemed like they were stretching to make the wildest possible joke, but there was no wit in any of them. It had a real "let's just throw it all out there and make it as absurd as possible" quality to it ("Let's make a parody of Ratatouille, except it it's a raccoon, and let's have a universe where they have hot dog fingers, and one where they only do karate with their pinky finger, and....."). The absurd comedy splashed into the fight sequences cheapened their stakes. It's a shame the different multiverses didn't give us more powerful perspectives of the different characters, wasting time on gag universes instead.
 
I also didn't like that the big philosophical question was posed and debated when the characters were inanimate yet also somehow sentient, animate rocks and pinatas. It felt like an attempt to do something bold and different, but the nonsensical presentation made it difficult for me to treat it's message seriously.

Some humor and even a little nonsensical absurdity would be fine, but the movie took it to such an extreme level in it's multiverses and fight sequences that it shifted my perceptual frame to think of the whole movie as a parody not to be taken seriously. As a result, I stopped caring as much about the outcome, in that I didn't really "feel" the universe was at stake or that the protagonists were in "real" danger. 

I know some would respond to this by saying the absurdity IS the point (life is absurd, we have to make our own meaning, etc.), but the reason why absurdity sucks in real life is that it undercuts meaning and authenticity. To me, this movie demonstrated that relationship perfectly, by undercutting its own meaning with too much absurdity.

Despite having seen it twice, I am struggling with exactly how to describe it - especially because the second time I watched it I wrote up some notes, but now I can't find them.  Ostensibly, we're following Evelyn (Michelle Yeoh) as she has a bit of breakdown around numerous issues surrounding her family (mostly her husband Waymond (Ke Huy Quan) and her daughter Joy (Stephanie Hsu)), business and finance.  

Oh, and the potential destruction of all existing parallel universes by a bagel that's topped with everything.

And, boy do these parallel universes display a wildly imaginative range of, well, everything everywhere all at once.  The flights of fancy that are entered here go waaay beyond anything that would occur to most people - there is some seriously mad stuff going on.  But, to the film's great credit, it's very grounded in human emotions which makes it surprisingly relatable and it also manages to wrap things up surprisingly well.  Obviously, this isn't to say that there aren't times that you have absolutely no idea what's going on!

Considering the huge range of actions and emotions on display, the film is really well acted with Michelle, Ke and Stephanie (who recently popped up in an episode of Poker Face) all excelling in their roles.  Jamie Lee Curtis is also a revelation as Deirdre Beaubeirdre, an amusingly grumpy tax inspector (in some of the universes, anyway).  I'm also going to mention Tallie Medal as Becky, who brings a pleasing level of normalcy to the film and Jenny Slate as Debbie The Dog Mom because we'll be meeting her in 2023 in a slightly higher profile role as the writer of Marcel The Shell With Shoes On.

It's interesting to note that after I complained that Avatar extended sequences unnecessarily, this film features one sequence that only features a couple of rocks "viewing" the scenery - and you'd say it goes on FAR too long, but it actually goes through that to become somewhat intriguing.  There's also an absolutely amazing 30 second scene which features more scenes that you get in some films.

For such a load of confusing nonsense, it did very well critically, winning seven Oscars including Best Picture, Director, Actress, Supporting Actor and Supporting Actress (for Jamie, although Stephanie was also nominated) as well as loads at other ceremonies - IGN reports it's the "most awarded film ever" (and I've no idea how you measure that!).  Here's a fine movie quiz question for you - no film has ever won all four acting Oscars but this was the third film to win three out of them,  What were the other two? (I wouldn't have got either of them!)

Yes, I haven't really described the film very well but it's pretty much a film that defies description.  It's also, in my opinion, utterly brilliant - the level of imagination, action and emotion on display throughout the film is way higher than most others, and it never suffers from any noticeable dip.  I have no idea why The Guardian left it off their list - they did like it, giving it four stars, but just not as much as other classics such as, well, at least half the films on their list that I've completely forgotten about.  If you've not seen it, then you should and you'll certainly be able to find it somewhere.

And the other two films which won three acting Oscars are A Streetcar Named Desire (1951) and Network (1976) - and I've never seen Network (shame on me!).

Buckle Up for Everything Everywhere All at Once: A Hilarious Multiverse Journey of Self-Discovery

Jump into the wild world of Evelyn Wang (Michelle Yeoh)! This stressed laundromat owner's life gets flipped upside down when she discovers the multiverse. Now, she must tap into her inner hero (think kung-fu master!) to battle an all-powerful villain across infinite realities.

But this is more than just a mind-bending adventure. It's a hilarious and heartwarming exploration of family, regret, and finding your purpose.

Yeoh shines as Evelyn, juggling outrageous alternate realities while confronting the complexities of her relationship with her husband (Ke Huy Quan) and daughter (Stephanie Hsu).

Get ready for a laugh riot as the film tackles sensitive topics like generational expectations, communication breakdowns, and the challenges of accepting oneself and others.

This rollercoaster ride through the multiverse is a must-see! It will leave you pondering the "everything bagel" of life, the importance of connection, and the power of embracing your true self, no matter the reality.

The movie is great, and I can't really say much more positive about it than has already been said. That's why I'm taking a different approach and looking at it from a different angle.

The negative reviews.

They show me that the film is pretty much perfect in what it's trying to achieve. So far, I haven't read or seen a single negative review that doesn't boil down to not understanding the film or finding it obscene, embarrassing, too fast, or over the top. It's like a good rock song in the '80s that's criticized by people who think Bon Jovi makes music that's too intense and just screams. Also, his music videos are too obscene because he shows a naked shoulder. That's not appropriate. Also, they don't understand the lyrics because he speaks in metaphors instead of saying directly what he means. Or it's often comparable to old people claiming that a movie is simply too quiet and everyone is mumbling because they don't admit to themselves that they've just gotten old and hard of hearing.

There are so many criticisms of EEAAO that are based solely on the fact that the film, for example, has a scene with a dildo and therefore is bad. Why is it bad? Well, because there's a dildo in it and weird things happen with it. End of story.

These are about as valid statements as "I don't like the movie because there are too many people eating pizza for breakfast." Why does that make the movie bad? "Well, because pizza isn't breakfast." Ultimately, it's just a deviation from the norm or personal preferences. If you don't like pizza for breakfast, that's no reason to completely dislike the person who enjoys pizza for breakfast.

And now without metaphor: A dildo in crazy and even obscene scenes doesn't make a movie bad just because you don't like it.

Everyone has the right to dislike the movie. That's not a problem. Generally, there are differences between good movies, bad movies, and movies that you simply don't like but are still good. But many people don't see that.

What I'm trying to say with this review is that the criticisms are somewhat powerless and only rate the film poorly based on personal preferences without any universally applicable points of criticism.

And thus, you recognize a good film.
